data.summary: Morello is Arm’s application-class CHERI prototype platform, providing real hardware for developing, porting and evaluating CHERI software.

_hardware.body:
Developed by Arm in collaboration with the [University of Cambridge](/organisations/university-of-cambridge/) and [SRI International](/organisations/sri/) through the UK Digital Security by Design (DSbD) programme, Morello brings CHERI capabilities to an application-class processor and development board.

It provides developers with a complete environment for exploring CHERI on real high-performance hardware, including operating systems, toolchains and substantial applications.

## What is Morello?
{: id="what-is-morello" }

![Arm Morello board](/assets/pages/adopt--assurance-and-adoption--case-studies/bfeebb3ac676-morello-board.webp){: .image-right }

The Morello platform includes:

- a prototype architecture based on AArch64 with CHERI capabilities
- the Morello processor and system-on-chip (SoC)
- the Morello development board
- supporting firmware, operating systems and development tools

Morello is one prototype implementation of CHERI, not CHERI itself. Other CHERI platforms, including CHERI-RISC-V and CHERIoT, use different architectures and software environments.

## Software environment
{: id="software-environment" }

The Morello ecosystem includes:

- CHERI-aware LLVM and Clang
- hybrid and pure-capability ABIs
- CheriBSD with a broad Unix user space
- CHERI-related Linux and Android work
- QEMU, debugging tools, libraries, language runtimes, and application ports

`cheribuild` is a common open-source route for building Morello LLVM, CheriBSD, disk images, and related tools from compatible source revisions.

## When should I use Morello?
{: id="when-to-choose-morello" }

Morello is particularly useful if you want to:

- develop and test CHERI software on real application-class hardware
- port substantial existing software to CHERI
- experiment with pure-capability software
- measure real hardware behaviour rather than simulator execution
- reproduce or extend an existing Morello project
- investigate Morello-specific ABI or architecture behaviour
- compare results across different CHERI environments

Morello was designed for research, development and evaluation rather than as a mass-market production processor. For new commercial products, developers should consider current CHERI platforms and their availability, support and lifecycle.

## Request a Morello board

The [CHERI Alliance](/organisations/cheri-alliance/) has **Morello boards available** for loan to organisations working on projects that can help advance CHERI development and adoption.

Boards are limited, so requests should explain clearly what you plan to do and why access to Morello hardware would be valuable.

### What to include in your request

Tell us about:

- Your project: What do you want to build, port, test or demonstrate?
- Its value: How could the work contribute to CHERI adoption, research, tools, software, demonstrations or the broader ecosystem?
- Why you need Morello: Explain why alternatives such as QEMU or other CHERI development boards are not sufficient for the project.
- Your organisation: Boards are loaned to organisations rather than individuals.
- Your team: Tell us briefly about your expertise, motivation and interest in contributing to the CHERI ecosystem.

--- 
[Contact the CHERI Alliance](/alliance/membership/contact/) to request a board
---

You can also find further information about the platform from [Arm's Morello page](https://www.arm.com/architecture/cpu/morello).

## Developing on Morello
{: id="developing-on-morello" }

A typical Morello project starts with a compatible software environment and known working example before moving on to your own software.

You should know whether the binaries you are working with are conventional, hybrid or pure capability, and keep the firmware, operating system, toolchain and ABI versions compatible.

For development, debugging and porting guidance, use the technical documentation associated with the software and platform version you are using.


## Strengths
{: id="strengths" }

Morello provides:

- real application-class CHERI hardware
- mature CheriBSD and LLVM/Clang integration
- an environment for porting substantial software
- a widely used platform for CHERI research and experimentation
- experience and evidence that can inform development on other CHERI platforms

## Constraints
{: id="constraints" }

- Morello is a prototype architecture and board
- Physical boards are less accessible than local simulation
- Its performance and encoding choices do not predict every future CHERI processor
- Software built specifically for the Morello ABI is not automatically portable to CHERI-RISC-V
- Long-term product support must be assessed separately from research and evaluation access

## A note about performance

The Arm Morello platform is a **research and prototyping system** designed to enable software development, porting, and evaluation of CHERI-based architectures. However, it is not representative of a production-quality CHERI implementation and should therefore not be used as the sole basis for assessing the performance overhead of CHERI.

Performance results obtained on Morello may reflect characteristics of the prototype hardware, development-stage toolchains, and implementation choices specific to the research platform, rather than the intrinsic cost of CHERI itself. Consequently, direct comparisons between Morello and conventional production processors can lead to misleading conclusions regarding CHERI performance overhead.

We recommend using Morello primarily for software development, compatibility testing, and functional evaluation. Once an application has been ported and validated, researchers should seek to corroborate performance results using additional CHERI platforms, implementations, simulators, or published results that better reflect production-oriented designs. Real-world workload measurements across multiple platforms provide a more reliable basis for understanding the true performance impact of CHERI. The CHERI Alliance can provide guidance on available platforms and benchmarking opportunities to support such evaluations.

Use the [Arm Morello resources](https://developer.arm.com/Architectures/Morello), [CheriBSD Getting Started](https://www.cheribsd.org/getting-started/), and [`cheribuild`](https://github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/cheribuild) for current technical instructions. For its place in the wider timeline, read [Morello History](/discover/history/morello-history/).

data.summary: Sonata is an accessible FPGA development platform for running CHERIoT firmware with real peripherals before moving to production silicon.

thumbnail.alt: CHERIoT processor on a Sonata board

_hardware.body:
Simulation is the quickest way to build a first CHERIoT application, but embedded development soon needs physical input and output. Developers must test timers, UARTs, storage, sensors, displays, and fault behaviour on hardware.

Sonata provides a purpose-built FPGA platform for that stage.

## What Sonata provides
{: id="what-sonata-provides" }

![CHERIoT processor on a Sonata board](/assets/pages/adopt--assurance-and-adoption--case-studies/645cc3b9a905-sonata-cheriot.webp){: .image-right }

Developed by [lowRISC](/organisations/lowrisc/), Sonata combines an FPGA implementation of a CHERIoT-capable system with a board and peripherals intended for embedded prototyping. It gives software developers a more direct route than assembling a processor core, system-on-chip design, and generic FPGA board themselves.

The platform is open and works with the CHERIoT real-time operating system (RTOS), software development kit (SDK), examples, and build flow. The CHERIoT project also provides a Sonata simulation route, allowing software to move between simulated and physical versions of a closely related platform.

## Typical workflow
{: id="typical-workflow" }

1. Clone the CHERIoT RTOS and its submodules.
2. Open the project’s development container.
3. Build a supplied example for the Sonata simulator.
4. Run its tests and capture expected output.
5. Change the board target to the documented Sonata hardware configuration.
6. Connect the board and deploy using the SDK’s run command.
7. Add peripherals and application compartments one at a time.

The exact board identifiers and deployment scripts follow the current RTOS and Sonata releases. Use the maintained documentation rather than an older copied command.

## What to prototype
{: id="what-to-prototype" }

Sonata is well suited to:

- compartmentalised network or protocol stacks
- secure update and boot workflows
- sensor and actuator control
- third-party library isolation
- key and credential services
- peripheral drivers
- fault containment and recovery demonstrations
- firmware-size and FPGA resource measurements

Its physical interfaces let developers test the parts that an instruction-set simulator cannot represent realistically.

## Simulator and board parity
{: id="simulator-and-board-parity" }

Starting with the Sonata simulator offers several advantages:

- no device access is needed for continuous integration
- faults and logs are easier to capture automatically
- every developer can reproduce the same baseline
- software changes can be separated from cable, flash, and peripheral issues

Repeat timing-sensitive and hardware-integration tests on the board. Simulation speed is not a processor performance measurement.

## Strengths
{: id="strengths" }

- Purpose-built for CHERIoT prototyping.
- Accessible development workflow through the CHERIoT SDK.
- Physical peripherals for realistic embedded experiments.
- Open platform resources and a corresponding simulation route.
- A bridge between software-only learning and commercial device integration.

## Constraints
{: id="constraints" }

- FPGA timing, power, and area differ from production silicon.
- The board’s peripheral set may not match the final product.
- A prototype bitstream or RTOS branch may change independently of a stable release.
- Product assurance must use the final core, system-on-chip, firmware, and hardware configuration.
- A successful Sonata prototype does not by itself establish supplier lifecycle or production-volume availability.

## Record the complete configuration
{: id="record-the-complete-configuration" }

For every result, capture:

- Sonata board and revision
- FPGA bitstream or system revision
- CHERIoT instruction-set architecture (ISA) and RTOS release
- SDK container and compiler version
- board configuration file
- firmware source revision
- connected peripherals and clock settings

Visit the [Sonata project documentation](https://sonata-system.github.io/sonata-system/) and the [CHERIoT getting-started guide](https://cheriot.org/book/getting_started.html) for current hardware and software instructions.

data.summary: The X730-MP4-Lux 1.0 record describes the certified application-processor core, its CHERI-RISC-V modes, verification evidence, and system-integration assumptions.

_hardware.body:
## Product information
{: id="product-information" }

The X730 is a commercially licensable 64-bit application-processor core implementing CHERI-RISC-V. The baseline design is described as an in-order, dual-issue, nine-stage processor with a memory-management unit, extended to handle capabilities and CHERI instructions.

![X730 block diagram](/assets/pages/adopt--assurance-and-adoption--cheri-enabled-products--x730/114ea730a8ce-x730-block-diagram.webp){: .image-full }

## Certification answers
{: id="certification-answers" }

### Q2 - What CHERI ISA do you implement and what extensions do you have?
{: id="q2---what-cheri-isa-do-you-implement-and-what-extensions-do-you-have" }

The X730 is an RVA22 compliant processor with the following optional/extra extensions.

| Extension | Version | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zfhmin | v1.0 | half precision floating point |
| Zam | v0.1 | Misaligned atomics |
| Zbkb | v1.0.1 | Bitmanip instructions for cryptography |
| Zbkc | v1.0.1 | Carry-less multiply instructions |
| Zkt | v1.0.1 | Data independent execution latency |
| Ss1p12 | v1.12 | Supervisor architecture |
| Svpbmt | v1.0 | Page-based memory types |
| Svinval | v1.0 | Fine-grained address translation cache invalidation |
| Sm1p12 | v1.12 | Machine architecture |
| Sdext | v1.0 | External debug interface |
| Sdtrig | v1.0 | Debug triggers |
| Zcheripurecap | v0.9.3 | CHERI-RISC-V Extension |
| Zcherihybrid | v0.9.3 | Integer pointer mode support |
| Zabhlrsc | v0.9.3 | Byte and half loads and stores |
| Zstid | v0.9.3 | Software thread identification |
| Zish4add | v0.9.3 | Addition using wider registers |
| Zcheripte | v0.9.3 | PTE control of capability storage |
| Zcherilevels | v0.9.3 | CHERI capability levels |
| Svyrg | v0.9.7 | 4-bit PTE scheme for revocation |

### How do you make sure that the HW does what it is supposed to do?
{: id="how-do-you-make-sure-that-the-hw-does-what-it-is-supposed-to-do" }

 Verification of X730 has been extensive. It has followed a strategy of deconstructing the design into its constituent components and major subsystems, then verifying those independently. This has been done with a mixture of formal property-based environments and simulation, and resulted in ~17 different verification environments, including:

- CHERI checks and calculations have their own set of formal proofs to ensure accuracy and robustness.
- The memory subsystem has its own simulation environment focused on data coherency in multi-core configurations.
- The execution pipeline is simulated in isolation, allowing all instruction semantics to be verified by randomised instruction streams against the RISC-V Sail model.
- Formal equivalence proofs are performed to ensure that power-saving techniques such as clock-gating do not change the functionality of the design.

These separate environments allow the verification of each component to explore corner cases far easier than if they were only tested when integrated into the full design. The layering of verification environments (like the CHERI formal and the full execution pipeline above) allows the detection and tracking of “escapes” from one layer to the next. These then drive the improvement of the verification.

All verification results are tracked against requirements to ensure that everything that has been specified has been covered by at least one of the environments and gaps do not form between environments. Codasip’s processes have been reviewed by TUV/SUD and 32-bit configurations generated from the same code-base has received ISO 26262 certification for use in automotive applications.

In total, over 40 person-years of engineering effort has been put into X730’s verification.

### Q3 - What operations can access memory without an explicit capability operand?
{: id="q3---what-operations-can-access-memory-without-an-explicit-capability-operand" }

In pure-cap mode: None.

In hybrid/integer mode: PCC and DDC are implicitly added to integer pointers.

Page table walks are not bounded by capabilities.

Capabilities are checked within their own virtual address space. The software that manages the address space is bound by capabilities (within its address space) but may abuse address translation to allow lesser privileged code to breach its isolation. Thus these software elements must form part of the trusted code base of the system.

Debug mode disables all CHERI checks. Debug mode is not expected to be active in normal operation. Debug mode can only be entered via RISC-V standard methods. SoC-level security controls are expected on the external debug interface.

### Q4 - What operations can set tags on arbitrary values?
{: id="q4---what-operations-can-set-tags-on-arbitrary-values" }

X730 only transforms tagged capabilities according to the proposed RVY extension, which does not allow any tagged values to be written to a register that are not derived from capabilities with equal or greater privilege. In addition, only aligned, capability-wide writes and reads preserve the tag from the register, and all other writes clear the capability tag.  There are therefore no instructions that can set a tag on arbitrary values in a register or overwrite a tagged value in memory with an arbitrary value without clearing the tag.

Beyond the scope of this certification, we have carefully engineered the memory subsystems to ensure that the commitment to memory of capabilities preserves atomicity with their tags.

### Q5 - How do you ensure integrity of tags with concurrent overlapping writes?
{: id="q5---how-do-you-ensure-integrity-of-tags-with-concurrent-overlapping-writes" }

Our CPU core has a single bus master for data accesses and so cannot make concurrent writes. When in a multi-core configuration the cores cannot make concurrent writes to the same cache line due to the coherent memory system. Cores can make concurrent writes to the same uncached memory address, and these are ordered by the L2 cache before being sent to the SoC memory system. The L2 cache treats the capabilities as atomic units that cannot be partially overwritten. The L2 cache, by its nature, cannot make concurrent accesses to the system memories.

### Q6 - How do you handle temporal safety?
{: id="q6---how-do-you-handle-temporal-safety" }

The X730 implements RV64Y Svyrg, which enables temporal safety for allocated memory in virtual address spaces: a supervisor can entirely remove access to freed virtual addresses before the memory is reallocated by placing freed memory regions in quarantine and using a background sweeper thread to find any dangling references before reallocation.

CHERI uses a combination of hardware and software to implement temporal safety on the MMU-based X730 core. CHERI allows temporal safety to be enforced by making it possible to accurately identify pointers, and check the memory which they are permitted to access. There have been various papers published on this topic (CHERIvoke, Cornucopia and Cornucopia Reloaded). Each offers improved performance over the previous paper. The X730 implements a 4-bit PTE scheme to accelerate revocation using the scheme from Cornucopia Reloaded allowing virtual memory pages to have their capabilities accurately tracked. It provides Capability Dirty Tracking to identify which pages have had capabilities stored to them, and a load barrier to prevent capabilities from being loaded from pages which have not yet been swept for stale capabilities which would allow use-after-reallocation vulnerabilities. Freed memory regions are held in quarantine until all stale capabilities which refer to them have been swept (located and invalidated).

### Q7 - What have you done to evaluate security of the CHERI properties of the system?
{: id="q7---what-have-you-done-to-evaluate-security-of-the-cheri-properties-of-the-system" }

- We perform formal verification of CHERI-related components within the microarchitecture to ensure compliance with the specification.
- We perform a security analysis of the microarchitecture (including CHERI-specific threat modelling) and generate a set of security requirements and mitigations for required behaviour. For example, this includes the expected behaviour during transient execution.
- We have a security test suite and fuzzing framework to cover known transient execution attacks, prediction-based non-transient execution attacks, cache attacks, timing attacks, etc.
- We evaluate out-of-context attacks e.g. the impact of RowHammer on CHERI capability tag storage.
- We run security test suites against OS and RTOS. e.g. the Juliet test suite as well as kernel test suites (such as syscall fuzzers) adapted for CHERI ABIs.
- Vulnerabities have been identified and resolved in both hardware and software (e.g. an incorrectly ordered bounds check during speculative execution)

### Q8 - What compilers do you support?
{: id="q8---what-compilers-do-you-support" }

LLVM19.1.7 Clang and Rust

data.summary: Bring CHERI hardware-enforced protection to Linux-based systems and applications.

_software.body:
**Linux** is at the heart of many products, platforms and services. CHERI Linux is the effort to extend CHERI support through the Linux software stack, allowing existing Linux environments to take advantage of capability-based memory protection.

Supporting CHERI involves more than enabling a processor and compiler. Capabilities must work correctly through the kernel, virtual memory, system calls, executable loading, libraries, debugging and the wider user-space environment.

## Why CHERI Linux?
{: id="why-cheri-linux" }

For organisations already building products and services around Linux, CHERI Linux provides a route towards adopting CHERI while retaining the familiar Linux ecosystem.

It is particularly relevant when you want to:

- bring CHERI to an existing Linux-based platform
- develop Linux applications for CHERI processors
- protect both applications and system software with CHERI capabilities
- reuse existing Linux interfaces, drivers and development practices
- evaluate CHERI for future Linux-based products
- contribute to making CHERI support available across the Linux ecosystem

## What needs to change?
{: id="what-needs-to-change" }

CHERI support reaches across the Linux software stack. Areas of development include:

- processor architecture support and boot
- capability register and process state
- virtual memory
- system calls and signals
- executable loading
- tracing and debugging
- device and driver interactions
- C libraries and dynamic loaders
- user-space and root-filesystem environments

Kernel support and pure-capability user space are closely related, but they are distinct areas of development. A kernel capable of running on CHERI hardware does not by itself provide a complete pure-capability Linux environment.

## Development environments
{: id="development-environments" }

A CHERI Linux development environment can bring together:

- a CHERI compiler and toolchain
- CHERI-enabled Linux kernel sources
- QEMU or another supported simulator
- user-space libraries and a root filesystem
- debugging and development tools
- an FPGA or physical processor platform when required

The exact environment depends on the processor architecture and implementation. Processor suppliers may also provide an integrated SDK containing compatible versions of these components.

## CHERI-RISC-V and other platforms
{: id="development-environments-2" }

CHERI Linux development includes work targeting CHERI-RISC-V, alongside experience gained from earlier Linux development for Morello.

Support varies between processor implementations and software configurations, so developers should use the kernel, toolchain, libraries and platform software recommended for their chosen target.

A minimal Linux system that boots on a CHERI processor and a broad pure-capability Linux environment are also different milestones. Application, library, package and driver coverage grows as more of the ecosystem is adapted and tested.

## From kernel support to applications
{: id="from-kernel-support-to-applications" }

Ultimately, CHERI Linux is about more than booting Linux on CHERI hardware.

For CHERI protection to extend through real workloads, capabilities need to be supported consistently across the operating system, system libraries, application interfaces and software packages.

This makes CHERI Linux relevant to both kernel and platform developers, who are enabling the underlying architecture, and application developers, who want to build and port software for CHERI-enabled Linux systems.

## Working towards common Linux support
{: id="working-towards-common-Linux-support" }

CHERI Linux is a cross-project effort rather than a single processor-specific port. The [CHERI Alliance Linux Working Group](/groups/cheri-linux-working-group/) brings organisations and developers together to coordinate priorities, share implementation experience and help drive convergence across CHERI architectures and platforms.

The longer-term goal is to reduce platform-specific fragmentation and establish common approaches that can support CHERI integration across the wider Linux ecosystem.

## Where CHERI Linux fits
{: id="where-cheri-linux-fits" }

Choose CHERI Linux when Linux APIs, drivers, applications or deployment environments are important to your target system.

Other CHERI operating-system environments serve complementary needs. For example:

- [CheriBSD](/software/cheribsd/) provides a mature environment for application-class CHERI research, software porting and pure-capability experimentation, and is a useful reference for bringing CHERI to other operating systems
- [CHERI-Zephyr](/software/cheri-zephyr/) provides another route for embedded and RTOS development

CHERI Linux is therefore particularly important for bringing CHERI into the large body of software and products already built around Linux.

## Project links
{: id="project-links" }

- [CHERI Roadmap for Linux](/linux-roadmap/)
- [CHERI Linux project documentation](https://cheri-linux.org/)
- [CHERI Alliance repositories](https://github.com/CHERI-Alliance)
- [CHERI Linux Working Group](/groups/cheri-linux-working-group/)

data.summary: Bring CHERI hardware-enforced protection to Zephyr-based embedded systems.

_software.body:
CHERI Zephyr brings capability-based memory protection to the Zephyr ecosystem, providing a route for developers who want to explore CHERI while retaining familiar Zephyr APIs, drivers, build tools and development practices.

Supporting CHERI involves more than enabling a processor and compiler. Capability protection also needs to work across the operating system, including threads, memory, interrupts, drivers and interactions between application and kernel code.

## Why CHERI Zephyr?
{: id="why-cheri-zephyr" }

Zephyr is already used as the software foundation for many embedded systems. CHERI-enabled Zephyr explores how these existing software environments can benefit from hardware-enforced memory protection without adopting an entirely different operating-system model.

It is particularly relevant when you want to:

- bring CHERI to an existing Zephyr-based project
- port existing embedded applications to CHERI
- retain familiar Zephyr APIs, drivers and development tools
- explore stronger isolation between software components
- evaluate CHERI for future embedded products
- contribute to CHERI support in the wider Zephyr ecosystem

## What needs to change?
{: id="what-needs-to-change" }

CHERI protection extends beyond the processor into parts of the operating system that create, store or use pointers and capabilities.

This includes areas such as:

- thread creation and context switching
- stacks and memory management
- user and kernel transitions
- interrupts and exceptions
- kernel objects and system interfaces
- drivers
- compiler and linker configuration
- capability faults and diagnostics

Together, these changes allow Zephyr software to make use of CHERI's hardware-enforced memory protection.

## Development environment
{: id="development-environment" }

CHERI Zephyr development brings together the CHERI processor architecture, compiler and toolchain, Zephyr kernel, board configurations, drivers, samples and tests.

Support is progressing at different pace depending on architectures, processors, boards, drivers and Zephyr configurations, so developers should use the software and platform combination recommended for their chosen CHERI target.

As support develops, the goal is not simply to boot Zephyr on a CHERI processor, but to extend meaningful capability protection through applications and the wider operating-system environment.

## Zephyr and CHERIoT
{: id="zephyr-and-cheriot" }

Both CHERI-enabled Zephyr and CHERIoT address embedded systems, but they provide different routes to adopting CHERI.

|  | CHERI-enabled Zephyr | CHERIoT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foundation | The Zephyr RTOS ecosystem | A hardware-software design built around CHERI |
| Existing interfaces | Zephyr APIs, drivers, Kconfig, west, and board support | CHERIoT SDK, RTOS, compartments, and xmake build system |
| Compartment model | Defined by the evolving CHERI Zephyr integration | Central to the platform architecture |
| Main attraction | Continuity with Zephyr software and devices | A security-first embedded model designed around capabilities |

The choice is therefore not simply about which platform is more mature. It depends on whether your priority is bringing CHERI to an existing embedded software ecosystem or adopting a platform designed around CHERI from the outset.

## Working towards broader Zephyr support
{: id="working-towards-broader-zephyr-support" }

The [CHERI Alliance Zephyr Working Group](/groups/cheri-zephyr/) coordinates collaboration around CHERI Zephyr, bringing together implementation work, platform support, testing and contributions.

A key objective is to reduce fragmentation between individual CHERI implementations and build common approaches that can support CHERI across the broader Zephyr ecosystem.

## Choosing CHERI Zephyr
{: id="choosing-cheri-zephyr" }

CHERI Zephyr is particularly useful when you want to:

- retain the Zephyr programming and development model
- investigate CHERI protection in an RTOS environment
- bring existing Zephyr applications and drivers to CHERI
- evaluate CHERI for embedded products
- use the Zephyr port as a reference for bringing CHERI to other RTOS environments
- contribute to common CHERI support for embedded software

For projects that instead want an embedded hardware and software platform designed around capability-based compartmentalisation from the outset, CHERIoT provides a complementary route.

{: id="project-links" }

data.summary: Develop and run complete applications on an operating system adapted for CHERI.

_software.body:
CheriBSD extends FreeBSD with support for CHERI, providing a complete application-class environment for developing, porting and testing CHERI software on CHERI-RISC-V and Arm Morello.

It brings CHERI capabilities through the operating system and software stack, allowing developers to work with real applications, libraries and services rather than isolated examples.

## Why use CheriBSD?
{: id="why-use-cheribsd" }

CheriBSD provides a familiar Unix environment in which developers can explore how existing software behaves when pointers become CHERI capabilities and hardware-enforced memory protection extends across applications and the operating system.

You can use CheriBSD to:

- develop and port applications to CHERI
- experiment with hybrid and pure-capability software
- build and test substantial existing C and C++ codebases
- investigate capability faults and compatibility issues
- work with libraries, networking, filesystems and operating-system services
- develop using QEMU or supported physical hardware

For many developers exploring application-class CHERI, CheriBSD provides the software environment in which the different parts of the CHERI ecosystem come together.

## Hybrid and pure-capability software
{: id="hybrid-and-pure-capability-software" }

CheriBSD supports both hybrid and pure-capability software models.

In a hybrid environment, conventional pointers and CHERI capabilities can coexist, providing a route for progressively adapting existing software.

In a pure-capability environment, language-visible pointers are represented as capabilities, allowing CHERI protection to be applied systematically throughout applications and supporting libraries.

CheriBSD's pure-capability environment, known as CheriABI, has enabled substantial existing software to be ported and tested, providing valuable experience of the compatibility issues that arise when moving existing code to capability-based systems.

## What does CheriBSD include?
{: id="what-does-cheribsd-include" }

CHERI support in a general-purpose operating system goes far beyond the processor and compiler. Capabilities need to work throughout the software stack.

CheriBSD integrates CHERI across areas including:

- the FreeBSD kernel
- hybrid and pure-capability ABIs
- system libraries
- executable loading and dynamic linking
- system calls, signals and faults
- debugging and developer tools
- third-party software packages
- supported simulators and hardware platforms

This provides a complete environment for exploring CHERI at application and system level.

## Development environments
{: id="development-environments" }

### CHERI-RISC-V and QEMU
{: id="cheri-risc-v-and-qemu" }

`cheribuild` provides an integrated route for building a compatible CHERI toolchain, QEMU, CheriBSD and disk image.

This allows developers to create a complete application-class CHERI development environment without requiring physical hardware, making it a practical starting point for software development and porting.

### Morello
{: id="morello" }

CheriBSD supports Morello's hybrid and pure-capability software environments.

Together with the corresponding CHERI compiler, firmware and platform support, Morello provides a physical application-class platform for developing and evaluating CHERI software.

### Other CHERI-RISC-V platforms
{: id="other-cheri-risc-v-platforms" }

CheriBSD can also run on supported CHERI-RISC-V processor and FPGA platforms where the architecture and system implementation provide the required operating-system support.

Support is platform-specific, so check the processor architecture, CheriBSD version and board configuration before selecting a hardware target.

## Porting software to CheriBSD
{: id="porting-software-to-cheribsd" }

One of CheriBSD's most important roles has been providing a realistic environment for understanding how existing software adapts to CHERI.

Many applications compile with relatively small changes, while others expose assumptions about:

- pointer sizes and representations
- converting between pointers and integers
- object bounds
- memory allocation
- application binary interfaces
- interactions with native libraries

These are often exactly the assumptions that need attention when moving existing software towards a pure-capability environment.

## Relationship to FreeBSD
{: id="relationship-to-freebsd" }

CheriBSD extends FreeBSD rather than defining a completely separate operating system. It retains familiar Unix interfaces, networking, filesystems, build infrastructure and source organisation while adding the architectural and software changes needed for CHERI.

Generally useful changes can be contributed to FreeBSD, while CHERI-specific architecture and ABI development can continue within CheriBSD.

A standard FreeBSD installation should therefore not be confused with a complete CheriBSD environment.

## Choosing CheriBSD
{: id="choosing-cheribsd" }

CheriBSD is particularly useful when you want to:

- develop application-class CHERI software
- port substantial existing applications
- explore pure-capability software
- investigate operating-system support for CHERI
- evaluate software on QEMU before moving to hardware
- compare software behaviour across CHERI platforms
- use CheriBSD as a reference for porting other operating systems to CHERI

CheriBSD is primarily a research and development platform for application-class CHERI, rather than a direct replacement for Linux or a single fixed product configuration. Its extensive integration of CHERI across the kernel, ABI, libraries and user space also makes it a useful reference for operating-system developers implementing CHERI support elsewhere.

For developers getting started, the natural route is cheribuild + QEMU + CheriBSD, before moving to an FPGA or physical CHERI platform when hardware-specific behaviour becomes important.

## Project links
{: id="project-links" }

- [`cheribuild`](https://github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/cheribuild)
- [CheriBSD source](https://github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/cheribsd)
- [CheriBSD Getting Started](https://www.cheribsd.org/getting-started/)
- [CheriBSD ports](https://github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/cheribsd-ports)

related-pages.description: A full-system CHERI environment with capability-aware faults, tracing, core dumps, and developer tools.

related-pages.title: QEMU Working Group

An embedded CHERI platform with compartment-aware firmware and diagnostic tooling.

data.summary: Understand CHERI faults and inspect capabilities alongside familiar program state.

_software.body:
CHERI adds information to pointers, including bounds, permissions and protected validity information. Capability-aware debugging tools make this state visible alongside familiar addresses, registers, variables, symbols and stack traces.

When CHERI prevents an invalid memory access, these tools can help developers understand what the program tried to do, which capability it used, and why the operation was rejected.

## Debugging capability faults
{: id="debugging-capability-faults" }

A CHERI capability fault occurs when software attempts an operation that is not permitted by the capability it is using.

Depending on the platform and tools, diagnostics may show information such as:

- the capability involved
- the attempted memory address and operation
- capability bounds
- permissions
- tag and sealing state
- the instruction that caused the fault
- the process, thread or compartment in which it occurred

This can make CHERI faults valuable during development: rather than allowing an invalid access to silently corrupt memory, the hardware can **stop** it at the point where protection is violated.

The exact diagnostics and terminology vary between CHERI platforms.

## GDB and LLDB
{: id="gdb-and-lldb" }

Capability-aware versions of GDB and LLDB extend familiar debugging workflows with support for CHERI capabilities.

Alongside source code, breakpoints, registers, memory and stack traces, supported debugger builds can expose capability registers and their associated bounds, permissions and state.

Debugger support depends on the target architecture, ABI and platform, so use the debugger supplied or recommended for your CHERI development environment.

## Debugging with QEMU
{: id="debugging-with-qemu" }

QEMU provides a convenient environment for investigating capability faults without requiring physical hardware.

It is particularly useful for:

- developing and debugging CHERI software
- reproducing capability faults
- remote debugging
- automated testing
- running tests consistently across development and continuous-integration environments

Because QEMU provides an architectural rather than physical implementation model, hardware-specific behaviour may require an FPGA or silicon platform.

## Operating-system and embedded diagnostics
{: id="operating-system-and-embedded-diagnostics" }

Different CHERI software environments integrate capability debugging in different ways.

- **CheriBSD** carries capability information through operating-system facilities such as faults, signals, core dumps and process debugging, providing an application-class environment for investigating CHERI software.
- **CHERI Linux** development similarly needs capability-aware kernel and user-space diagnostic support as the platform evolves.
- **CHERIoT** provides diagnostics in a compartment-oriented embedded environment, where faults can be investigated in the context of individual software compartments and the authority available to them.

## Inspecting binaries
{: id="inspecting-binaries" }

Debugging sometimes starts before the program runs. CHERI-aware binary tools can help developers inspect how capabilities are represented in compiled software.

Tools such as `llvm-readelf`, `llvm-objdump`, and `nm` can be used, with appropriate CHERI support, to examine areas such as symbols, sections, relocations, generated instructions and capability-related information in executable files.

These tools can be particularly useful when investigating compiler, linker, loader or ABI issues.

## Choosing debugging tools
{: id="choosing-debugging-tools" }

Capability-aware debugging is currently closely tied to the underlying CHERI architecture, ABI, operating system and software environment. A conventional debugger may be able to display the raw contents of a capability-sized value without understanding all of its CHERI-specific state.

## From fault to fix
{: id="from-fault-to-fix" }

CHERI changes an important part of the debugging experience: memory errors that might otherwise cause corruption or appear much later can instead become explicit capability faults.

Capability-aware diagnostics help developers trace those faults back to incorrect pointer use, insufficient authority or other software assumptions, making debugging tools an important part of the CHERI development environment.

## Project links
{: id="project-links" }

- [CHERI Alliance GDB](https://github.com/CHERI-Alliance/gdb)
- [CTSRD-CHERI GDB](https://github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/gdb)
- [`cheribuild`](https://github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/cheribuild)
- [CHERIoT Programmer’s Guide](https://cheriot.org/book/)

data.summary: Compile C and C++ software for CHERI-enabled platforms.

_software.body:
LLVM and Clang provide the compiler foundation for much of the CHERI software ecosystem. They translate ordinary language-level operations, such as accessing objects through pointers, into code that uses CHERI capabilities and the protection they provide.

Clang is the C and C++ compiler developers interact with, while LLVM provides the underlying compiler infrastructure and code generation.

## What changes when compiling for CHERI?
{: id="what-changes-when-compiling-for-cheri" }

CHERI hardware uses capabilities to control how software accesses memory. The compiler plays an important role in creating and preserving those capabilities as it translates source code into machine code.

Depending on the target platform, Clang can support:

- capability-based pointers
- hybrid and pure-capability software
- capability bounds and permissions
- CHERI-specific operations and intrinsics
- calling conventions and application binary interfaces (ABIs)
- diagnostics that identify assumptions in existing code that may not work correctly with capabilities

In many cases, existing C and C++ software can be compiled for CHERI with relatively small changes, while code that makes assumptions about pointers, memory layouts or integer conversions may require more attention.

## Hybrid and pure-capability builds
{: id="hybrid-and-pure-capability-builds" }

CHERI platforms can support different ways of introducing capabilities into existing software.

In a hybrid environment, conventional pointers can coexist with CHERI capabilities. This can be useful when bringing up platforms and progressively adapting existing software.

In a pure-capability environment, pointers are represented as CHERI capabilities throughout applications and supporting software, providing stronger and more systematic enforcement.

The available models and ABIs depend on the target platform. Morello, application-class CHERI-RISC-V and CHERIoT therefore use toolchains configured for their respective architectures and software environments.

## CHERI toolchain routes
{: id="cheri-toolchain-routes" }

### CheriBSD and CHERI-RISC-V
{: id="cheribsd-and-cheri-risc-v" }

The `cheribuild` environment brings together a compatible LLVM and Clang toolchain, system headers, linker, QEMU, and CheriBSD image. It supports application-class CHERI-RISC-V work across hybrid and pure-capability software configurations.

### Morello
{: id="morello" }

Morello uses an Arm-based CHERI compiler and ABI together with its corresponding system software and platform support.

The Morello software environment has been widely used to develop and port applications to CHERI and explore the transition between conventional and pure-capability software.

### CHERIoT
{: id="cheriot" }

The CHERIoT SDK uses a Clang-based toolchain aligned with the CHERIoT instruction set, RTOS, compartment model, linker, and firmware build system.

### Mainline LLVM
{: id="mainline-llvm" }

Parts of CHERI support are already present in upstream LLVM, while complete target support can still depend on platform-specific branches and releases. A key focus for the CHERI Alliance is bringing this work together, driving convergence across CHERI platforms and helping move towards common, upstream LLVM support.

## Bounds and compatibility
{: id="bounds-and-compatibility" }

CHERI compilers can use information about objects and allocations to create capabilities with appropriate bounds and permissions.

How tightly those bounds are applied can vary between platforms and configurations, balancing stronger protection with compatibility requirements. As a result, compiler version, target architecture, ABI and software environment all matter when building or comparing CHERI software.

Code that assumes that pointers and integers have the same representation, or relies heavily on particular object layouts or pointer manipulation, may need additional attention when moving to a CHERI target.

## Getting started
{: id="getting-started" }

For most developers, there is no need to build or understand the CHERI compiler infrastructure itself. Start with the toolchain supplied or recommended for your chosen platform.

For application-class CHERI development, `cheribuild` provides an integrated route to LLVM/Clang, QEMU and CheriBSD. For embedded development, use the toolchain and SDK associated with the target platform, such as CHERIoT.

From there, the next step is to [compile existing software](/guides/port-existing-software/), understand any compatibility warnings or errors, and progressively adapt the code to make effective use of CHERI's protection.


## Project links
{: id="project-links" }

- [`cheribuild`](https://github.com/CTSRD-CHERI/cheribuild)
- [LLVM project](https://llvm.org/)
- [CHERIoT Programmer’s Guide](https://cheriot.org/book/)

data.summary: CHERI software support is reported by platform, architecture, ABI, operating system, package set, and project revision rather than by one ecosystem-wide percentage.

_software.body:
CHERI porting is not one centrally versioned programme. It spans processor architectures, compilers, operating systems, real-time environments, runtimes, applications, packages, emulators, and hardware platforms maintained by different projects.

## Why status varies
{: id="why-status-varies" }

A project can support capability instructions without providing a pure-capability application ABI. An operating system can boot before it has broad driver or package coverage. A library can compile while still depending on untested pointer assumptions. These are different forms of progress rather than steps on one universal scale.

Status claims also change with architecture revisions, toolchain branches, kernel versions, board support, and release processes.

## Current areas of public work
{: id="current-areas-of-public-work" }

- **CheriBSD** combines a capability-aware kernel, hybrid and pure-capability user space, developer tools, and a substantial history of third-party software ports.
- **CHERI Linux** spans kernel, user-space, toolchain, and platform work across active branches and processor environments.
- **CHERIoT** provides an embedded architecture, RTOS, compartment model, SDK, and growing application ecosystem designed together.
- **CHERI-Zephyr and FreeRTOS** bring capability work into established embedded operating-system communities.
- **Rust and managed runtimes** extend CHERI beyond established C and C++ toolchains, with support varying between target projects.

## Where status is recorded
{: id="where-status-is-recorded" }

The most current information lives with the project that owns a branch, release, SDK, board configuration, package set, or test environment. Alliance Working Groups connect several of these projects and publish roadmaps, repositories, articles, and event updates where shared coordination is useful.

This page describes the structure of that landscape. Individual platform and software pages link to the corresponding public project records.

data.summary: Develop Rust software for CHERI-enabled platforms.

_software.body:
Rust and CHERI provide complementary approaches to memory safety. Rust provides **language-level** protections, while CHERI adds hardware-enforced protection **at run time**, including around unsafe code, native interfaces and compartment boundaries.

For a broader explanation of how the two technologies complement each other, see the [CHERI and Rust technical overview](/build/technology/cheri-and-rust-technical/).

## Rust on CHERI
{: id="rust-on-cheri" }

Supporting Rust on a CHERI platform involves more than adding a compiler target. The compiler, pointer representation, application binary interface (ABI), libraries, allocator, operating-system interfaces, native bindings, debugger and build tools all need to work with CHERI capabilities.

In particular, CHERI capability pointers may differ from conventional pointers in size and representation. Code that makes assumptions about pointer sizes, integer conversions or data layouts may therefore need attention.

## What about unsafe Rust?
{: id="what-about-unsafe-rust" }

Safe Rust prevents many memory-safety errors before software runs, but real systems may also contain unsafe Rust, native libraries, operating-system components or code written in other languages.

On a CHERI platform, hardware capabilities can constrain the memory and permissions available to this code, providing an additional layer of protection where Rust's language-level guarantees do not apply.

CHERI does not make unsafe Rust automatically safe, or replace Rust's rules around aliasing, lifetimes and initialisation. Instead, the two provide complementary protection at different layers.

## Working with native code
{: id="working-with-native-code" }

Rust applications often need to interact with existing C or C++ libraries, operating-system services and other native components through foreign-function interfaces (FFIs).

On CHERI platforms, these interfaces also need to account for capability pointers, including their bounds and permissions, as well as ABI, memory-allocation, object-layout and ownership requirements.

This makes mixed-language interfaces an important area to test when bringing existing Rust software to CHERI.

## Current platform routes
{: id="current-platform-routes" }

### Morello and CheriBSD
{: id="morello-and-cheribsd" }

Rust work for Morello has included freestanding and CheriBSD environments, compiler targets, libraries and native interfaces.

These environments provide a route for exploring Rust on an application-class CHERI platform. Particular configurations may depend on project-specific toolchains and versions.

### CHERI-RISC-V
{: id="cheri-risc-v" }

Rust support is also being developed for CHERI-RISC-V, including pure-capability environments and operating-system integration.

Available compiler targets, libraries, package support and operating-system environments vary between projects and implementations.

### CHERIoT
{: id="cheriot" }

Rust support is developing within the CHERIoT embedded ecosystem.

The established CHERIoT development environment is centred on its C and C++ SDK, while Rust work is extending support across the compiler, runtime and compartment interfaces.

## Check your target environment
{: id="check-your-target-environment" }

Rust support is not yet uniform across all CHERI platforms. Before starting development, check:

- which CHERI architecture and processor are targeted
- which Rust compiler and target are supported
- whether the required core and standard libraries are available
- which ABI and pointer representation are used
- which operating system or runtime is supported
- whether Cargo and required packages work with the target
- which debugging and testing tools are available
- how native libraries and interfaces are supported

Pinning the toolchain and platform versions used by a project can also help keep builds and tests reproducible.

## Rust + CHERI collaboration
{: id="rust-cheri-collaboration" }

Rust support across CHERI is continuing to evolve across compiler, operating-system, embedded and hardware projects. 

The [Rust + CHERI Working Group](/groups/rust-plus-cheri/) connects this work across the CHERI Alliance and aims for convergence and compatibility. [CHERI and Rust](/discover/why-cheri/cheri-and-rust/) provides the broader architectural context.

data.summary: Develop and test CHERI software and systems without physical hardware.

_software.body:
Simulation is often the easiest way to get started with CHERI. It lets you develop, port and test software before you have access to CHERI hardware.

Different simulators serve different purposes. Some run complete operating systems and applications relatively quickly, while others provide detailed models of the CHERI architecture or a particular processor implementation.

## Which simulator do I need?
{: id="which-simulator-do-i-need" }

For most **software developers**, QEMU is a good place to start. It can run complete CHERI software environments and is well suited to application development, porting and automated testing.

For **architecture and hardware developers**, more detailed models are available:

- **Sail models** provide an executable reference for CHERI instruction behaviour and architecture development
- **RTL simulation** runs the processor's hardware design, exposing implementation-level behaviour
- **Compiled hardware models**, using tools such as Verilator, can provide a faster way to simulate some hardware designs
- **Supplier simulators** may provide models tailored to particular commercial processors and development environments

The right choice depends on what you want to learn.

## QEMU for software development
{: id="qemu-for-software-development" }

CHERI-enabled QEMU provides a convenient way to run complete CHERI software environments without physical hardware. `cheribuild` can build QEMU together with matching development tools, operating systems and disk images.

Use QEMU to:

- boot CHERI-enabled operating systems
- develop and test applications
- port software to pure-capability environments
- run automated test suites
- investigate capability faults
- develop without physical CHERI hardware

QEMU models architectural behaviour rather than a particular processor's physical implementation. It should therefore not be used to predict processor performance or hardware characteristics such as detailed cache, speculation or timing behaviour.

## Sail for architecture development
{: id="sail-for-architecture-development" }

**Sail** is a formal model that provides executable descriptions of instruction-set behaviour and is used in CHERI architecture development, reference simulation, test generation and formal reasoning.

It is particularly useful when the question is "What should this CHERI instruction do?" rather than "How quickly will this software run?"

Sail models can also provide an independent reference against which processor implementations can be compared.

When using an executable architecture model, make sure its CHERI instruction-set architecture (ISA) version matches the system or implementation you are testing.

## CHERIoT simulation
{: id="cheriot-simulation" }

The CHERIoT development environment provides simulation routes for both architecture and processor-implementation models.

This allows developers to run compartmentalised firmware in simulation before moving to an FPGA or production hardware, and to test software at different levels of abstraction during development.

## RTL simulation for hardware development
{: id="rtl-simulation-for-hardware-development" }

**Register-transfer-level (RTL)** simulation runs the processor's actual hardware description and is primarily useful to processor and hardware developers.

It can help investigate:

- CHERI instruction implementation
- capability-tag storage and propagation
- caches and memory interfaces
- exceptions and interrupts
- reset and privilege behaviour
- buses and peripheral integration

RTL simulation provides much more implementation detail than QEMU, but is significantly slower. It is therefore generally better suited to focused hardware tests and smaller software workloads than running complete applications and operating systems.

Compiled implementation models, using tools such as **Verilator**, can provide another route for running some hardware designs more quickly while retaining implementation-specific behaviour.

## Choosing the right simulator
{: id="choosing-the-right-simulator" }

Start with the question you are trying to answer:

- Develop or port software? Start with QEMU or the recommended simulator for your target platform
- Check architectural behaviour? Use an executable reference model such as Sail
- Validate a processor implementation? Use RTL simulation or a compiled implementation model
- Evaluate a particular processor? Check whether its supplier provides a simulator and matching SDK
- Need to test hardware integration or peripherals? Consider moving from simulation to an FPGA platform

Whichever route you choose, check that the simulator, CHERI ISA version, compiler and software environment are compatible.

## Moving to hardware
{: id="moving-to-hardware" }

Simulation lets you start developing with CHERI without waiting for physical hardware.

Use [Run CHERI in Simulation](/guides/run-cheri-in-simulation/) for a first practical setup, and move to [FPGA Platforms](/hardware/fpga-platforms/) when the question depends on hardware implementation.

data.title: ✅ Certification WG
data.summary: Develops shared thinking around certification criteria, assurance needs, evidence, and the operation of Alliance certification programmes.

_groups.body:
The Certification Program Working Group is responsible for defining the [CHERI Enabled](/adopt/assurance-and-adoption/about-cheri-enabled/) program for CHERI products:

- **Guidelines** – We define the guidelines and rules that products must follow to be certified. This includes setting the standards and criteria that products need to meet
- **Processes** – We outline the processes and conditions necessary for product approval. This involves creating a structured pathway that products must go through to achieve certification
- **Support** – We provide support to assist companies in certifying their products. This support can come in various forms, including documents, test suites, or any other relevant deliverables that facilitate the certification process
- **Systems** – We help coordinate the implementation of systems required to manage the certification and lists of certified products. This ensures that there is an organized and accessible record of all products that have met the certification criteria
- **Communication** – We also define the message to explain the value of the program and clarify what to expect from certified products

The group aims to continuously improve the certification program. This involves regularly reviewing and updating the guidelines, processes, and systems to enhance efficiency, effectiveness, and relevance

Overall, the working group plays a crucial role in ensuring the compliance and compatibility of certified CHERI products to make sure that users can trust the CHERI logo to guarantee a correct implementation of the technology.

data.title: ©️ CHERI C/C++ WG
data.summary: Coordinating portable C and C++ support for CHERI platforms.

_groups.body:
The C/C++ Working Group aims to ensure portability for C and C++ code written for CHERI platforms.

CHERI provides memory safety for C-like languages. Every CHERI implementation will trap on buffer overflows in C and many will trap on use-after-free. Beyond that, C compilers provide builtins for CHERI-specific and CHERI-implementation-specific features, additional headers, and so on.

This working group has two overlapping goals:

- To coordinate between CHERI C/C++ implementations to ensure portability.
- To work with ISO WG14 and WG21 to ensure long-term alignment of the C and C++ standards with CHERI.

data.title: 4️⃣ CHERI for seL4 WG
data.summary: Coordinates work at the intersection of CHERI capabilities, seL4, Microkit, verified kernels, and capability-oriented system design.

_groups.body:
The CHERI for seL4 Working Group focuses on the integration and combination of the two technologies. The objectives of the seL4 WG are:

- Consolidate existing efforts trying to port seL4 to CHERI
- Coordinate open-source development efforts around CHERI-seL4\*
- Have a single CHERI-seL4 (kernel) to reduce confusions with upstreaming and the seL4 community
- Sync updates, events, demos, etc. around CHERI-seL4

*Please note that CHERI-seL4 is experimental and isn’t formally verified or upstream yet.*

data.title: 🆓 CHERI FreeRTOS WG
data.summary: Coordinates common approaches to memory protection, compartmentalisation, interfaces, and platform support for FreeRTOS on CHERI systems.

_groups.body: The FreeRTOS Working Group aims to provide a common ground for CHERI-based solutions on FreeRTOS across the Alliance.

data.title: ⬛️ CHERI in SoC WG
data.summary: Brings together the architecture, integration, and verification questions involved in adding CHERI to a system-on-chip.

_groups.body:
The CHERI in SoC Working Group focuses on defining and standardizing what needs to be included in a system to support CHERI, and to provide useful resources to speed the wider adoption of CHERI within chiplets and SoCs.

The resources we deliver will help accelerate:

- Learning what is involved when creating a device or system that supports CHERI.
- Understanding the different levels of CHERI support, and what guarantees they can offer.
- Making the right trade-offs and choices for the devices and systems being developed.
- Extending or innovating technologies to better enable CHERI at the system level.

data.title: 🐧 CHERI Linux WG
data.summary: Coordinates priorities, cross-architecture requirements, implementation experience, and contribution routes for CHERI support in Linux.

_groups.body:
The CHERI Linux Working Group defines and prioritises a roadmap for the porting of Linux to CHERI, while stimulating open-source communities to work on these element.

The technical [CHERI Linux page](/software/cheri-linux/) explains the wider software stack and current development.

data.title: 📋 CHERI + Safety WG
data.summary: Explores how CHERI mechanisms, implementation evidence, and system integration relate to functional safety and assurance needs.

_groups.body: The Safety Working Group focuses on implementing safety standards for CHERI hardware to leverage its memory safety and fine-grained protection capabilities, thereby enhancing the security and safety of safety-critical systems.

data.title: 🐦 CHERI QEMU WG
data.summary: Coordinates CHERI support in QEMU so developers have maintained, testable emulation aligned with current architectures and platforms.

_groups.body: The QEMU Working Group focuses on the support of CHERI within the QEMU software emulator.

data.title: 🤖 CHERI Virtual Machines WG
data.summary: Examines how language runtimes, managed environments, and virtual machines can use and preserve CHERI capabilities.

_groups.body: The CHERI Virtual Machines Working Group adapts VMs and language runtimes for CHERI platforms, exploring optimisations for enhanced security and functionality

data.title: 🪁 CHERI Zephyr WG
data.summary: Coordinates CHERI support for Zephyr across architecture ports, kernel and user interfaces, drivers, tooling, and supported platforms.

_groups.body:
The CHERI Zephyr Working Group focuses on adapting Zephyr to leverage CHERI’s memory safety and fine-grained protection capabilities, enhancing security for embedded and IoT system.

The [CHERI Zephyr software ecosystem page](/software/cheri-zephyr/) provides the technical overview and links to current public development resources.

data.title: 📣 Marketing WG
data.summary: Coordinates accurate CHERI messaging, shared material, campaigns, events, and communication across the Alliance ecosystem.

_groups.body:
CHERI needs explanations that are accurate, useful to different audiences, and clear about the maturity of the technology. The group coordinates shared messages and material so Alliance activity can be communicated consistently without flattening important technical distinctions.

Activity can include editorial planning, member stories, event promotion, campaign material, and review of public explanations. The group works alongside the [Promotion & Ambassador Program](/groups/promotion-and-ambassador-program/) while retaining a distinct focus on Alliance-wide communication.

data.title: 👮 MMU-less Systems WG
data.summary: Examines CHERI protection and compartmentalisation for systems that share an address space and do not depend on a conventional memory-management unit.

_groups.body:
The goal of this WG is to discuss designs for a broad range of CHERI systems where the common theme is that they operate on a shared single address space between processes. The three main categories of systems that I have in mind are:

- Embedded single-address space physical memory systems. This includes systems like CHERIoT.
- Application-class single-address space physical memory systems. This expects large physical memories where processes reside permanently because dynamically managing process memory in this setting is difficult, and supporting disk swap may not be easy.
- Application-class single-address space virtual memory systems. This uses virtual memory solely to virtualize physical memory, facilitating dynamic process memory management and supporting disk swap, while capabilities manage all access control.

It is important to discuss both the hardware and software aspects of such a design. For instance, a traditional POSIX fork call cannot work in a single-address space setting. In general, we should discuss how to redesign system calls to work in this single-address space setting.

We will also propose and discuss other designs that broadly fall into the category of CHERI-based single-address space systems, or systems that don’t require traditional MMUs.

data.title: 🛠️ OS Support & Portability WG
data.summary: Connects operating-system ports, shared interfaces, terminology, and documentation across CHERI architectures and software projects.

_groups.body:
The OS Support & Portability Working Group brings together contributors focused on supporting and documenting the process of adapting both open-source and commercial operating systems for CHERI.

The group aims to publish practical guides, recommendations, and code examples to aid porting efforts, while also acting as a temporary home for work on less common OSes.

In addition, the group collects and shares general insights from OS porting that may benefit the wider CHERI software porting community.

## Relationship to other groups
{: id="relationship-to-other-groups" }

Relevant Alliance groups include [CHERI Linux](/groups/cheri-linux-working-group/), [CHERI FreeRTOS](/groups/cheri-freertos/), [CHERI Zephyr](/groups/cheri-zephyr/), [CHERI for seL4](/groups/cheri-for-sel4/), and [MMU-less Systems](/groups/mmu-less-systems/). Each retains its own technical scope while contributing experience relevant to portability.

data.title: 🪪 Promotion & Ambassador Program WG
data.summary: Helping the CHERI ecosystem communicate clearly, consistently, and effectively.

_groups.body:
CHERI is relevant to a wide range of audiences, from developers and researchers to product teams, policymakers, educators, and security leaders. This group coordinates targeted outreach, coordination and community-engagement activities that help those audiences understand what CHERI is, where it is being used, and how it can support more secure computing.

The group supports promotion of the CHERI Alliance and development of the ambassador programme, helping expand awareness of CHERI across different regions, sectors, and communities.

## The Ambassador programme
{: id="the-ambassador-programme" }

The group manages and supports the [Ambassador programme](/alliance/leadership/ambassadors/), helping ambassadors share accurate information about CHERI within their professional, technical, academic, and regional networks.

data.title: 💾 Repository Management WG
data.summary: Develops consistent practices for the structure, maintenance, contribution, quality, and stewardship of shared Alliance repositories and technical collateral.

_groups.body:
The Repository Management Working Group focuses on defining rules for participation, maintenance and contribution to CHERI open-source projects, managed or not by the Alliance. The repository management working group helps structure the CHERI-Alliance GitHub organisation.

Our aim is to have high quality resources available and to foster collaboration in the community. We also want to set up organisation-wide rules that improve the quality for our community.

data.title: ⚙️ Rust + CHERI WG
data.summary: Combining memory-safe software and hardware-enforced protection.

_groups.body:
The Rust + CHERI Working Group explores how Rust and CHERI can work together to strengthen software security. By combining Rust’s memory-safety guarantees with CHERI’s hardware-enforced memory protection and compartmentalisation capabilities, the group helps advance practical approaches to building more resilient systems.

The [Rust software ecosystem page](/software/rust/) explains the relationships between Rust and CHERI.

data.summary: Build compartments by mapping authority first, then give each component only the memory, services, and entry points required for its task.

_guides.body:
Memory-safe code can still be over-privileged. A parser may correctly read the input it receives but have no reason to access encryption keys, update controls, or unrelated application state. A compartment boundary limits what the component can reach even if it is buggy or compromised.

The hard part is not adding the boundary instruction. It is deciding which authority must cross it.

## Choose a useful first boundary
{: id="choose-a-useful-first-boundary" }

Good first compartments have a narrow purpose and an existing interface. Examples include:

- image, document, or protocol parsers
- network stacks and packet-processing stages
- cryptographic services
- device drivers
- update verification
- third-party libraries
- key-value storage

A source-directory split alone does not create a useful security boundary. A compartment should correspond to assets and threats that can be described and tested.

## Describe the authority each component needs
{: id="describe-the-authority-each-component-needs" }

Before writing code, list what the component needs:

- **Input packet:** The parser needs to read one packet, so it receives a read-only capability bounded to that packet.
- **Output record:** The parser needs to return validated data, so it receives a writable capability bounded to one output record.
- **Log service:** The parser may submit a structured diagnostic event through a sealed service entry.
- **Key store:** The parser does not need keys, so it receives no capability for the key store.
- **Update service:** The parser does not change firmware, so it receives no capability for the update service.

This list describes the proposed security policy. Review it before implementation and keep it with the tests.

## Design a narrow interface
{: id="design-a-narrow-interface" }

Prefer interfaces that pass bounded data and small, well-defined values:

~~~
int parse_message(const unsigned char *input,
                  size_t input_length,
                  struct parsed_message *output);
~~~

The interface should define:

- ownership and lifetime of each object
- whether memory is read-only, writable, or transferred
- maximum sizes and permitted overlap
- valid return values and fault behaviour
- whether the callee may retain a capability after returning
- which service capabilities the callee may invoke

Passing a pointer to a large application context is convenient but usually grants too much authority.

## Derive, do not widen
{: id="derive-do-not-widen" }

The caller should derive a narrower capability from authority it already holds:

1. restrict the bounds to the specific object
2. remove permissions the callee does not need
3. pass only the required service entry points
4. avoid ambient globals that bypass the interface

CHERI capabilities can normally be reduced but not amplified. The design should not depend on the callee inventing authority later.

## Select the platform mechanism
{: id="select-the-platform-mechanism" }

Compartment application programming interfaces (APIs) differ by environment:

- **The CHERIoT real-time operating system (RTOS)** defines firmware compartments, imported and exported entry points, shared objects, and sealed service capabilities through its software development kit (SDK) and build model.
- **CheriBSD** supports several compartmentalisation approaches for applications and operating-system components, including capability-aware process and in-process models.
- **Other CHERI operating systems and runtimes** may provide their own call gates, switchers, sealing conventions, or service interfaces.

Use the platform’s maintained mechanism. A calling convention assembled from raw sealing operations is appropriate only when the architecture work itself is the goal.

## Test the negative cases
{: id="test-the-negative-cases" }

A compartment test suite must show what fails:

- read one byte before and after an input buffer
- write through a read-only capability
- call an entry point that was not granted
- retain and reuse authority beyond its documented lifetime
- pass a capability with missing or excessive permissions
- corrupt untrusted input and confirm recovery behaviour
- attempt to reach a known secret outside the compartment

Check not only that the processor faults, but also what the system does next. Does it terminate one compartment, restart a service, reset the device, or stop the whole application? Availability is part of the design.

## Measure boundary cost
{: id="measure-boundary-cost" }

Fine-grained compartments trade reduced authority for transition and communication overhead. Measure:

- call latency and throughput
- copied versus shared data
- stack and metadata memory
- scheduler or switcher activity
- cache effects on representative hardware
- recovery cost after a fault

If a boundary is too expensive, first reduce call frequency or batch data. Removing the security boundary should not be the automatic optimisation.

## Review checklist
{: id="review-checklist" }

- Every granted capability appears in the authority record.
- No undocumented global or inherited authority bypasses the interface.
- Bounds and permissions are narrower than the caller’s own authority where possible.
- Lifetimes and capability retention are explicit.
- Negative tests prove denied actions remain denied.
- Fault handling preserves the required availability and safety behaviour.
- Performance results name the platform, software revision, and workload.

For an embedded worked path, use the [CHERIoT Programmer’s Guide](https://cheriot.org/book/). For the underlying mechanism, read [Compartmentalisation](/build/technology/compartmentalisation/) and [Sealing](/build/technology/sealing/).
