data.summary: CHERI gives policy discussions an additional route to memory safety: hardware-enforced protection for low-level and existing software, with finer-grained containment.

_policies.body:
Memory safety policy often centres on language change, vulnerability reduction, or secure development practice. CHERI broadens that discussion by protecting memory at the processor and supporting compartments with limited authority.

Its relevance is greatest where established native code will remain in use, where process isolation is too coarse or unavailable, and where one compromised component sits close to more valuable functions.

## Briefing: memory safety has more than one route
{: id="briefing-memory-safety-has-more-than-one-route" }

Memory-safe languages can prevent broad classes of defects and are an important foundation for new software. CHERI addresses low-level and existing code that may not move to a new language quickly. The two approaches can coexist in one product.

Testing, hardening, process isolation, virtual machines, updates, and vulnerability management also remain necessary. CHERI’s distinctive contribution is that the processor can reject memory access outside a capability’s bounds or permissions, while compartments can limit the authority that remains after compromise.

This makes CHERI relevant to a portfolio of memory-safety measures rather than a universal replacement for them.

## Briefing: adoption depends on an ecosystem
{: id="briefing-adoption-depends-on-an-ecosystem" }

A processor feature becomes useful in products through toolchains, operating systems, libraries, runtimes, debugging, training, test platforms, and assurance. CHERI’s path from research through Morello, CheriBSD, CHERIoT, RISC-V work, and commercial processor intellectual property shows that these surrounding layers are developing together.

Shared specifications, open software, compliance tests, and available development platforms reduce the amount of work repeated by each adopter. Commercial products and public certification records make the technology easier to compare with a real product need.

## Briefing: outcomes matter more than labels
{: id="briefing-outcomes-matter-more-than-labels" }

“CHERI-enabled” can describe very different levels of protection. A processor core may implement the architecture correctly, while a complete product may additionally run capability-aware software and use compartments throughout its design.

The meaningful outcome is the scope: which code uses capabilities, what memory and services each component can reach, which paths sit outside normal enforcement, and how the boundary behaves when an access is denied.

This is also why the CHERI Enabled programme is product-specific. Its public records connect the mark to a named version and submitted evidence rather than treating the technology name as a general security certificate.

## Briefing: containment supports resilience
{: id="briefing-containment-supports-resilience" }

Memory protection can stop an invalid operation. Compartmentalisation can prevent the affected component from reaching unrelated data or functions. Together, these properties can reduce the chance that one software flaw becomes a system-wide event.

For essential services, fault response remains part of the result. A capability fault may lead to restart, failover, degraded operation, or outage depending on the wider architecture. CHERI strengthens an internal boundary; availability and recovery remain system properties.

## Briefing: why CHERI may be a good fit
{: id="briefing-why-cheri-may-be-a-good-fit" }

The strongest policy case appears where four conditions meet:

- memory-unsafe software remains necessary;
- that software processes untrusted data or operates with significant authority;
- replacing it or placing it behind heavyweight isolation is impractical;
- the consequence of compromise extends beyond the component itself.

In those circumstances, CHERI offers a practical bridge between today’s software and stronger secure-by-design expectations. It can preserve valuable low-level code while changing what that code is permitted to access and how far a compromise can travel.

The Alliance provides technical explanation and connects policy organisations with the wider CHERI ecosystem. Legal interpretation remains with the relevant authorities and qualified advisers.

## GENERAL DATA PROTECTION REGULATION (GDPR)

We are a Data Controller of your information.

CHERI Alliance legal basis for collecting and using the personal information described in this Privacy Policy depends on the Personal Information we collect and the specific context in which we collect the information:

- CHERI Alliance needs to perform a contract with you,

CHERI Alliance will retain your personal information only for as long as is necessary for the purposes set out in this Privacy Policy. We will retain and use your information to the extent necessary to comply with our legal obligations, resolve disputes, and enforce our policies. Our Privacy Policy was generated with the help of [GDPR Privacy Policy Generator](https://www.gdprprivacynotice.com/) and the [GDPR Privacy Policy Generator](https://www.gdprcontracts.com/privacy-policy-generator/).

If you are a resident of the European Economic Area (EEA), you have certain data protection rights. If you wish to be informed what Personal Information we hold about you and if you want it to be removed from our systems, please contact us.

In certain circumstances, you have the following data protection rights:

- The right to access, update or to delete the information we have on you.
- The right of rectification.
- The right to object.
- The right of restriction.
- The right to data portability.
- The right to withdraw consent.

## LOG FILES

CHERI Alliance follows a standard procedure of using log files. These files log visitors when they visit websites. All hosting companies do this and a part of hosting services’ analytics. The information collected by log files include internet protocol (IP) addresses, browser type, Internet Service Provider (ISP), date and time stamp, referring/exit pages, and possibly the number of clicks. These are not linked to any information that is personally identifiable. The purpose of the information is for analyzing trends, administering the site, tracking users’ movement on the website, and gathering demographic information.

## PRIVACY POLICIES

You may consult this list to find the Privacy Policy for each of the advertising partners of CHERI Alliance.

Third-party ad servers or ad networks use technologies like cookies, JavaScript, or Web Beacons that are used in their respective advertisements and links that appear on CHERI Alliance, which are sent directly to users’ browsers. They automatically receive your IP address when this occurs. These technologies are used to measure the effectiveness of their advertising campaigns and/or to personalize the advertising content that you see on websites that you visit.

Note that CHERI Alliance has no access to or control over these cookies that are used by third-party advertisers.

## THIRD PARTY PRIVACY POLICIES

CHERI Alliance ‘s Privacy Policy does not apply to other advertisers or websites. Thus, we are advising you to consult the respective Privacy Policies of these third-party ad servers for more detailed information. It may include their practices and instructions about how to opt-out of certain options.

You can choose to disable cookies through your individual browser options. To know more detailed information about cookie management with specific web browsers, it can be found at the browsers’ respective websites.

## CHILDREN’S INFORMATION

CHERI Alliance does not knowingly collect any Personal Identifiable Information from children under the age of 13. If you think that your child provided this kind of information on our website, we strongly encourage you to contact us immediately and we will do our best efforts to promptly remove such information from our records.

## ONLINE PRIVACY POLICY ONLY

Our Privacy Policy applies only to our online activities and is valid for visitors to our website with regards to the information that they shared and/or collected in CHERI Alliance. This policy is not applicable to any information collected offline or via channels other than this website.

## CONSENT

By using our website, you hereby consent to our Privacy Policy and agree to its terms.

_policies.body:
![pdf](/assets/shared/source-assets/d63b7eac09b7-pdf-file-icon.webp){: .image-left .image-inline } Download the [CHERI Alliance Trademark Policy](/assets/shared/source-assets/d904a00cfb15-trademark-policy.pdf) – The PDF is the official version. The text is reproduced below for convenience, but if there is any difference between the two versions, the PDF takes precedence.

---

## Preamble
{: id="preamble" }

The CHERI Alliance is committed to promoting awareness and understanding of CHERI technology, especially in academic, educational, and informational contexts. This Trademark Policy is designed to ensure that the use of our trademarks is consistent with our mission, protects the integrity of our brand, and ensures that CHERI marks are only associated with genuine CHERI technology or CHERI Alliance-backed projects. Use of CHERI marks should not imply endorsement, affiliation, or certification unless authorized.

This Trademark Policy applies universally — not only to CHERI Alliance members, but also to non-members, including individuals, academic institutions, open-source projects, commercial entities, and other organizations – for the use of the CHERI name or visual assets.

By adhering to this policy, we aim to foster a community that respects and accurately represents the CHERI brand.

## Definitions
{: id="definitions" }

- **Nominative Fair Use:** Use of a trademark to refer to the trademarked product or technology itself, in a way that is not misleading or suggestive of endorsement.
- **Sublicense:** A written agreement granting permission to use CHERI marks beyond Nominative Fair Use, usually for branding or integration.
- **Written Permission** refers to explicit, documented approval from the CHERI Alliance, granted via email or formal letter by an authorized representative. It must clearly specify the scope, duration, and conditions of the approved use.

## Trademark Usage Rules
{: id="trademark-usage-rules" }

### CHERI ® name
{: id="cheri--name" }

Authorized for “Nominative Fair Use,” – meaning use of the trademark solely to truthfully describe or refer to the CHERI technology itself, the CHERI Alliance or its publications or projects, without suggesting any endorsement or affiliation.

For uses outside of Nominative Fair Use, a Sublicense or Written Permission from the CHERI Alliance is required.

When used in formal documents, the ® or ™ symbol must be included for the first mention, but the symbol is not required in informal communication (e.g. emails, blogs, discussions), or non-commercial academic contexts.

### Logos
{: id="logos" }

| --- | --- |
| ![CHERI mark](/assets/shared/source-assets/514789203a81-cheri-mark.webp){: .image-full } | **CHERI mark** Reserved for CHERI Alliance documentation and projects, or CHERI Certified products and services, especially when space constraints prevent the use of the CHERI Certified logo (e.g., on a chip package). |
| ![CHERI mark](/assets/shared/source-assets/e4cf8af68585-cheri-logo.webp){: .image-full } | **CHERI logo**  Permitted for use in CHERI Alliance documentation and projects, or under a Sublicense from the CHERI Alliance. Nominative Fair Use is authorized for discussions about CHERI technology without implying endorsement. |
| ![CHERI mark](/assets/shared/source-assets/edeb264ff3b7-cheri-member.webp){: .image-full } | **CHERI Alliance Member logo**  Reserved for use in any media by current, active CHERI Alliance members. |
| ![CHERI mark](/assets/shared/source-assets/213ed31db863-cheri-founder.webp){: .image-full } | **CHERI Alliance Founder logo** Reserved for use in any media by founding members of the CHERI Alliance, that are current, active members. |
| ![CHERI mark](/assets/shared/source-assets/031e517df8f0-cheri-enabled.webp){: .image-full } | **CHERI certification logo** Reserved for products and services that incorporate CHERI technology and have successfully obtained written approval from the CHERI Alliance certification program. |

The logos referred to above are illustrative examples. All official variations, including color schemes, proportions, text variations, and usage guidelines, are detailed in the CHERI Alliance Branding Guidelines. Always refer to the latest version of the Branding Guidelines for accurate and approved logo variations.

## Academic Use
{: id="academic-use" }

The CHERI Alliance recognizes the importance of academic freedom and encourages the use of its trademarks in academic settings, such as in papers, slides, and posters, provided that such use complies with the principles of Nominative Fair Use and includes one of the following attribution notes:

- “CHERI” and the CHERI logo are trademarks of the CHERI Alliance. This work refers to CHERI technology with permission and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the CHERI Alliance unless explicitly stated. See cheri-alliance.github.io
- “CHERI” and the CHERI logo are trademarks of the CHERI Alliance. See cheri-alliance.github.io

## Additional Rules
{: id="additional-rules" }

1. **Sublicense for Product Names:** Use of “CHERI” in product names (e.g., “CHERIBoard” or “CHERIChip”) requires a Sublicense.
2. **Written Permission for Open Source Projects:** Written Permission from the CHERI Alliance is necessary to use CHERI in the name of an open-source project. The definition of “open source” is detailed on the CHERI Alliance Website.
3. **No Logo Modification:** CHERI logos must not be altered, distorted, or combined with other marks or logos.
4. **Positive Use:** CHERI marks must not be used in misleading, defamatory, or derogatory contexts.
5. **Respect for Certification Program:** Use of terms such as “CHERI Certified,” “CHERI Compliant,” “CHERI Approved,” or any similar phrase that suggests certification, approval, or endorsement by the CHERI Alliance is strictly prohibited unless the product or service has received written approval through the CHERI Certification Program. Only the terms and logo specified by the Certification Program may be used for officially certified products and services.
6. **Adherence to Branding Guidelines:** All uses of CHERI marks must comply with the CHERI Alliance’s Branding Guidelines.
7. **Genuine Representation:** Ensure that the use of CHERI trademarks genuinely represents the involvement or inclusion of CHERI technology in the product or project.

## Enforcement
{: id="enforcement" }

The CHERI Alliance reserves the right to take action in cases of misuse of its trademarks. This may include requiring corrective steps, revoking Sublicenses, or initiating legal action to protect the integrity of the CHERI marks.

## Contact and Permissions
{: id="contact-and-permissions" }

For questions about this policy or to request Written Permission or a Sublicense, please [contact the CHERI Alliance Trademark Team](/alliance/membership/contact/).

## Updates
{: id="updates" }

This policy may be updated periodically. We will notify the public of any substantive changes. Continued use of CHERI marks after updates indicates acceptance of the revised terms. The latest version will be published on this page.

data.title: The CHERI Enabled Programme
data.summary: Independent review. Transparent evidence. Greater confidence.

pages.body:
The **CHERI Enabled** programme helps organisations demonstrate how a product implements CHERI technology. Certified products receive a public certification record describing what was assessed, the supporting evidence, and the scope of the certification.

| --- | --- |
| [![CHERI Enabled logo](/assets/shared/cheri-enabled/be89fa8f9b81-cheri-enabled.webp){: .image-full }](/adopt/assurance-and-adoption/cheri-enabled-products/) | See all the [CHERI Enabled products](/adopt/assurance-and-adoption/cheri-enabled-products/) |

## Why CHERI Enabled matters
{: id="why-cheri-enabled-matters" }

As CHERI adoption grows, products may implement CHERI in very different ways. CHERI Enabled helps organisations move beyond marketing claims by providing:

- A defined product and version
- A documented certification scope
- Reviewed technical evidence
- A public certification record
- A common basis for comparing products

For buyers, this reduces uncertainty. For product developers, it provides an independent way to demonstrate implementation quality and build confidence in security claims.

## How certification works
{: id="how-certification-works" }

![Certification Process](/assets/shared/source-assets/8651dcf7d9cf-certification-process.webp){: .image-full }

Products are assessed through a structured review process:

- Define the product and certification scope
- Submit evidence
- Participate in technical reviews and interviews
- Receive a certification decision
- Get a certification record and authorisation to use the CHERI Enabled mark
- Renew certification as products and requirements evolve

Updated or derivative products may follow a streamlined reassessment process.

## What certification evaluates
{: id="what-certification-evaluates" }

Certification reviews evidence relating to:

- How CHERI is implemented
- The protection provided by the product
- Verification and testing evidence
- Known limitations and integration considerations

The resulting certification record helps customers understand what has been assessed and what security properties the product aims to provide.

## Scope and limitations
{: id="scope-and-limitations" }

Certification represents the Alliance’s assessment of the submitted evidence. It **does not** guarantee complete product security, replace product assurance activities, or automatically extend to systems, applications, or products outside the certified scope.

Security outcomes always depend on how technology is integrated, configured, and maintained.

## Keeping certification relevant
{: id="keeping-certification-relevant" }

The programme will expand over time as the CHERI ecosystem grows, introducing additional product categories, requirements, and assessment criteria. Certifications are therefore reviewed every two years to help ensure that records remain aligned with current programme requirements.

Read the [current programme specifications](/assets/shared/source-assets/611b980d082a-certification-program-v1.pdf).

## Fees
{: id="fees" }

- First certification: £3,000 (£1,000 for CHERI Alliance members)
- Recertification: £1,500 (£500 for CHERI Alliance members)

The recertification fee also applies to derivative products.

## Apply for certification
{: id="apply-for-certification" }

CHERI Enabled certification helps organisations:

- Demonstrate implementation quality
- Build customer and partner confidence
- Support procurement and assurance activities
- Differentiate products in a growing CHERI ecosystem

Ready to certify a product? [Contact the CHERI Alliance](/alliance/membership/contact/) to start the process.

data.summary: CHERI can strengthen assurance by turning intended memory and component boundaries into processor-enforced properties that can be described and tested.

pages.body:
Assurance explains why a defined security or safety claim can be trusted. Certification records a judgement under a particular scheme. CHERI can contribute to both because it provides concrete properties about memory access and software authority, but neither follows from the presence of a CHERI-capable processor alone.

## Why CHERI can strengthen an assurance case
{: id="why-cheri-can-strengthen-an-assurance-case" }

In a conventional system, a software boundary may depend on coding rules, review, and the assumption that every pointer is used correctly. CHERI can place part of that boundary in the processor. Capabilities carry bounds and permissions, and compartments can receive a limited set of memory and services.

This supports claims with a defined subject and outcome, such as:

> In this configuration, the packet parser can access only its assigned buffers and the services exposed through its compartment interface.

That statement is narrower than “the product is secure,” but it is also far more useful. The protected component, permitted authority, and expected enforcement can all be connected to implementation evidence.

## Evidence across the system
{: id="evidence-across-the-system" }

CHERI-related assurance can draw on several layers:

- **Architecture:** the instruction-set specification, security model, capability rules, and behaviour when a check fails.
- **Hardware:** design verification, compliance testing, protection of capability tags, privileged paths, and debug behaviour.
- **Toolchain:** compiler behaviour, supported language models, conformance results, known limitations, and reproducible builds.
- **Software:** the code covered by capabilities, compartment configuration, interfaces, test results, and handling of unsafe operations.
- **Integration:** boot, devices, direct memory access, operating-system services, updates, monitoring, and fault response.
- **Product lifecycle:** traceable requirements, vulnerability handling, regression testing, maintenance, and recorded residual risk.

Evidence at one layer does not establish the others. A processor core can implement CHERI correctly while a wider system still includes direct-memory-access devices, debug paths, unsafe configuration, or software outside capability protection.

## Where this can be a good fit
{: id="where-this-can-be-a-good-fit" }

CHERI is relevant to assurance when a product depends on native code and its case includes claims about memory separation, least authority, or containment after compromise. It can be particularly valuable where components of different trust or assurance levels share an address space.

The fit is not limited to safety-certified products. Buyers and operators of general-purpose systems can also benefit from evidence that explains which software is protected, what it can reach, and what happens when a capability check fails.

## Certification remains scoped
{: id="certification-remains-scoped" }

Sector certification depends on the product, claims, standards, evidence, independence, and operating context. CHERI can contribute architectural and test evidence to that process; it does not replace the process or determine its outcome.

The Alliance’s [CHERI Enabled programme](/adopt/assurance-and-adoption/about-cheri-enabled/) has a specific purpose. It identifies named products whose submitted evidence supports the correct application of CHERI security principles. It is not a certificate for the overall security or safety of every system containing that product.

## Assurance over time
{: id="assurance-over-time" }

A claim remains meaningful when it is tied to the exact processor, architecture profile, toolchain, execution mode, software version, compartment design, and configuration. Changes to any of these may alter the evidence or the authority available to a component.

This specificity is one of CHERI’s strengths. It replaces a broad promise of “hardware security” with properties that can be bounded, inspected, tested, and maintained as part of the wider product assurance case.

data.summary: Applying CHERI in real products and platforms

pages.body:
From experimental research systems to commercial processor IP, CHERI has been applied across a growing range of platforms. These case studies illustrate how capability-based protection can be integrated into existing software, embedded devices, and modern processor architectures.

No single project can represent every possible use case. Together, however, these examples demonstrate that capability protection can coexist with substantial software stacks, resource-constrained devices, and existing C and C++ code.

| Project | Demonstrates |
| --- | --- |
| Morello | CHERI at application and server scale |
| CheriBSD | Protection of large existing software stacks |
| CHERIoT | CHERI for constrained embedded systems |
| Codasip X730 | Commercially application-class CHERI processor |

## Morello: a complete experimental stack
{: id="morello-a-complete-experimental-stack" }

The [Arm Morello programme](https://www.arm.com/architecture/cpu/morello) demonstrated that CHERI concepts can scale to a modern **high-performance 64-bit processor** and support real operating systems, toolchains, and applications.

Morello gave research and industry teams a realistic platform for porting operating systems and applications, examining compatibility, and measuring performance. It showed that CHERI could be applied to the most demanding high-performance processors.

Morello remains an experimental platform. Its importance lies in the full-stack evidence and experience it created, not in representing a production Arm architecture.

![Arm Morello board](/assets/pages/adopt--assurance-and-adoption--case-studies/bfeebb3ac676-morello-board.webp){: .image-full }

## CheriBSD: established software at operating-system scale
{: id="cheribsd-established-software-at-operating-system-scale" }

[CheriBSD](https://www.cheribsd.org/) demonstrates how a large existing operating system (FreeBSD, from the [FreeBSD foundation](/organisations/freebsd-foundation/)) can be adapted to take advantage of CHERI protection.

This work also showed how to perform a software migration, porting a large C codebase incrementally. The operating-system environment also provides a base for running and studying substantial applications.

This makes CheriBSD relevant to products that depend on mature native software and need evidence about the cost and effect of protecting it.

## CHERIoT: protection for small embedded devices
{: id="cheriot-protection-for-small-embedded-devices" }

[CHERIoT](https://cheriot.org/) brings CHERI protection to resource-constrained embedded systems and microcontrollers. The CHERIoT platform combines a 32-bit CHERI-RISC-V architecture, processor core, toolchain, and real-time operating system. It is designed around small compartments that do not trust one another and can communicate through controlled interfaces.

CHERIoT shows why CHERI can fit microcontrollers that lack the memory-management hardware used for process isolation on larger systems. It also combines capability protection with mechanisms intended to support temporal memory safety in constrained devices.

The `cheriot-ibex` core has been certified under the [CHERI Enabled programme](/adopt/assurance-and-adoption/about-cheri-enabled/).

![CHERIoT processor on a Sonata board](/assets/pages/adopt--assurance-and-adoption--case-studies/645cc3b9a905-sonata-cheriot.webp){: .image-full }

## CHERI in commercial processor products
{: id="cheri-in-commercial-processor-products" }

Codasip has [decided to adopt CHERI](/news/why-codasip-went-all-in-on-cheri/) throughout its whole line of products. X730-MP4-Lux is the first commercial 64-bit application-class processor implementing CHERI-RISC-V. It has been certified under the [CHERI Enabled programme](/adopt/assurance-and-adoption/about-cheri-enabled/) and can run rich operating systems like CheriBSD or Linux.

This demonstrates that CHERI processor technology is available now for commercial system-on-chip designs.

![Codasip X730 on FPGA](/assets/pages/adopt--assurance-and-adoption--case-studies/e8738d5ec725-codasip-prime-kit.webp){: .image-full }

## What these case studies demonstrate
{: id="what-these-case-studies-demonstrate" }

Together, these examples show that CHERI is not limited to a single class of system. CHERI has been applied to the whole spectrum of computing applications:

- From the most **constrained embedded** devices to traditional **application-class** and large **high-performance** systems
- From tiny real-time operating systems to rich multi-user operating systems
- In open-source platforms and commercial processor products
- While reusing substantial existing C and C++ software

While each project has different goals and constraints, all demonstrate how capability protection can be introduced into real hardware and software systems, across the diversity of use cases, while reusing existing software. These examples also demonstrate that CHERI can often be introduced while **reusing** significant amounts of existing **software**, reducing the need for complete rewrites.

The examples also show that CHERI is an ecosystem change rather than one processor feature. These projects have demonstrated mature toolchains, operating systems, libraries, runtimes, and debugging support, showing readiness for product development.

data.summary: CHERI adoption can range from protecting one exposed component to moving a complete platform, allowing cost and benefit to follow the scope of change.

pages.body:
Adopting CHERI does not imply rewriting an entire product. The scope can range from one library or service to an operating system and full software stack. This matters because the cost of migration can be matched to the part of a system where memory protection or containment has the greatest value.

## Different forms of adoption
{: id="different-forms-of-adoption" }

CHERI supports more than one transition model:

- **Targeted compartments** place selected components behind restricted interfaces, limiting their access to the rest of a system.
- **Hybrid systems** allow conventional pointers and capabilities to coexist, which supports gradual change and compatibility with software that has not yet moved.
- **Pure-capability systems** represent pointers as capabilities throughout the protected environment, providing broader and more consistent enforcement.
- **New CHERI-native designs** build capability boundaries into a platform from the outset, as seen in embedded systems such as CHERIoT.

These models offer different levels of coverage. A narrower change can reduce initial disruption, while a pure-capability environment exposes more unsafe assumptions and places more software under hardware enforcement.

## Where migration work appears
{: id="where-migration-work-appears" }

Much existing C and C++ code compiles with limited change. Work tends to concentrate in areas that treat pointers as unstructured numbers or depend on a specific pointer layout. Examples include custom allocators, hand-written assembly, device interfaces, serialisation code, and programs that store flags in unused pointer bits.

Costs can arise across several parts of a product:

- processor intellectual property, hardware, boards, simulators, and operating-system support;
- toolchains, build systems, continuous integration, debuggers, and analysis tools;
- source changes, third-party dependencies, assembly, and compartment interfaces;
- performance, memory, power, timing, and compatibility testing;
- training, documentation, assurance, supplier support, and long-term maintenance.

The shape of those costs is highly product-specific. A self-contained parser may be a modest port, while a low-level runtime or large codebase with unusual memory handling may require deeper work.

## Why incremental migration can fit
{: id="why-incremental-migration-can-fit" }

CHERI protection can be introduced at natural product boundaries: a new processor generation, an updated gateway, a replaceable service, or a component already due for substantial change. A representative component can reveal toolchain maturity, porting effort, and platform overhead before the same approach appears elsewhere in a product family.

This staged characteristic is important for long-lived and safety-related products. Existing releases can remain supported while new variants gain capability protection, and evidence can accumulate without making a whole estate depend on one migration event.

## Existing software remains part of the value
{: id="existing-software-remains-part-of-the-value" }

CHERI is unusual among memory-safety approaches because it can protect low-level software while retaining its language, algorithms, and much of its structure. That does not remove all porting work, but it changes the choice from “keep the code or gain stronger protection” to a broader set of options.

Third-party software remains an important factor. An upstream CHERI port can spread maintenance across a community, while a private patch, replacement component, or compartment boundary creates a different cost profile. The relevant question is not only whether the code runs, but how its protected form will be maintained across the product lifetime.

## Cost in context
{: id="cost-in-context" }

Migration cost is best understood beside the cost of the risk it addresses. Products with little native code, short lives, or strong existing isolation may see limited benefit. Products that combine exposed C or C++ code, valuable assets, broad component authority, and many years of support can present a much stronger fit.

The [porting overview](/guides/port-existing-software/) describes the technical patterns that influence effort, and [Choose a Platform](/guides/choose-a-platform/) explains the available execution environments.

data.title: The Cost of Memory Unsafety

data.summary: Reduce Risk. Protect Investment. Build Trust.

pages.body:
From emergency patches and delayed releases to service disruption and loss of trust, memory-unsafe software can affect organisations long after a product ships.

CHERI helps reduce that risk by making many memory-safety errors impossible to exploit and limiting the impact of those that remain.

## The Hidden Cost of Memory Vulnerabilities
{: id="the-hidden-cost-of-memory-vulnerabilities" }

When a memory-safety vulnerability is found, fixing the bug is often the smallest part of the cost.

![Vulnerability handling process](/assets/shared/source-assets/55d113947b39-vulnerability-handling.webp){: .image-full }

A memory-safety vulnerability can trigger **costly** investigations, regulatory reporting, emergency patching, customer support activity, compliance work, and roadmap **delays**, consuming resources long after the original bug has been fixed.

Even when no attack occurs, the investigation and remediation effort consumes time, resources, and budget. Even worse, with incoming regulations (including the [Cyber Resilience Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act) in Europe), there is an obligation and pressure to fix problem in a given time, potentially disrupting development roadmaps.

A recent study showed that 21 new Linux vulnerabilities are discovered **per day** (see [our Webinar](/events/webinar-cheri-cra-compliance/) on this topic)… This is worth investigating new solutions!

## Why This Matters Now
{: id="why-this-matters-now" }

Memory-safety vulnerabilities continue to account most serious software vulnerabilities.

At the same time:

- software is becoming more connected
- products remain deployed for longer
- regulatory expectations are increasing
- governments are placing greater emphasis on memory safety and secure-by-design practices

For many organisations, reducing memory-safety risk is becoming a **strategic objective** rather than simply an engineering concern. This is highlighted in [CISA’s case for memory-safe roadmaps](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/case-memory-safe-roadmaps).

## What CHERI Changes
{: id="what-cheri-changes" }

### From Mitigating Attacks to Preventing Them
{: id="from-mitigating-attacks-to-preventing-them" }

Traditional defences often just make memory vulnerabilities harder to exploit, until attackers find how to bypass them. CHERI changes the model.

By enforcing memory access rules directly in hardware, CHERI can **prevent** many invalid memory accesses from succeeding in the first place.

Combined with compartmentalisation, CHERI can also limit how far an attacker can move when a component is compromised.

### Key benefits
{: id="key-benefits" }

- Reduce exposure to memory-safety vulnerabilities
- Limit the impact of software compromises
- Protect existing C and C++ investments
- Improve resilience of long-lived products
- Support secure-by-design strategies

## The Business Outcome
{: id="the-business-outcome" }

Spend Less Time Responding. Spend More Time Innovating.

The goal is not simply to prevent individual vulnerabilities. It is to reduce the operational burden that memory vulnerabilities create throughout a product’s lifecycle.

By helping organisations detect faults earlier, contain compromises, and protect existing software investments, CHERI can help teams:

- reduce security risk
- improve product resilience
- simplify long-term support
- maintain customer trust
- focus resources on innovation rather than emergency response

data.summary: Turn stronger security into lasting business value.

pages.body:
Security investments create value throughout a product’s lifecycle. The benefits rarely appear as a single saving. Instead, they accumulate through avoided vulnerabilities, reduced engineering time for emergency response, and products that remain secure and supportable for longer.

CHERI helps deliver this value by reducing cyber risk, limiting the impact of compromise, and extending the lifetime of critical software investments.

## Value Across the Lifecycle
{: id="value-across-the-lifecycle" }

### Design
{: id="design" }

Building security in from the start is usually more effective and less costly than adding it later. CHERI provides hardware-enforced protection and compartmentalisation that help create more resilient system architectures. Like encryption and authentication, CHERI is an essential security capability that can be incorporated into products from the outset.

### Development
{: id="development" }

Finding defects earlier reduces cost and risk. CHERI can help developers discover invalid memory accesses very quickly during development and testing, making some issues easier to diagnose and fix.

### Verification
{: id="verification" }

CHERI provides concrete security properties that can be tested, evaluated, and documented, helping organisations demonstrate that appropriate protections are in place.

### Operations
{: id="operations" }

By preventing many memory-safety vulnerabilities from becoming successful exploits and limiting the reach of compromised software components, CHERI can help reduce operational risk and improve resilience.

### Maintenance
{: id="maintenance" }

Products often remain in service for many years. CHERI can help reduce support and remediation effort by limiting the consequences of vulnerabilities and improving fault isolation.

## Understanding ROI
{: id="understanding-roi" }

Adopting CHERI involves an initial investment, which may include new hardware, software adaptation, integration, and training. In many cases, this can be aligned with an existing product or platform refresh cycle.

Depending on the case, this could mean:

- Switching to a CHERI processor when designing a chip
- Porting existing software - which is often a [straightforward engineering task](/discover/understand/cheri-and-existing-software/)
- Changing some development habits for software developers
- Using CHERI chips when designing a product
- Requesting CHERI products instead of less secure ones

The return on CHERI is not measured only by incidents that never happen. Organisations can also benefit from:

- Reduced engineering effort spent investigating vulnerabilities
- Faster remediation and response times
- Lower operational disruption
- Reduced maintenance and support costs
- Reuse of assurance activities across product generations
- Longer useful life for software and platforms

These benefits can often be observed long before a major security incident is avoided.

For product vendors, stronger security can also create value through increased customer confidence, easier procurement conversations, and differentiation in security-conscious markets.

## Beyond Cost Reduction
{: id="beyond-cost-reduction" }

CHERI can also help organisations:

- Meet customer security expectations
- Support secure-by-design objectives
- Respond to emerging regulatory requirements
- Build trust with customers and stakeholders
- Differentiate products in security-conscious markets

As security becomes an increasingly important factor in purchasing, procurement, and regulation, these benefits can translate into commercial advantage as well as risk reduction.

## Where the Value Is Strongest
{: id="where-the-value-is-strongest" }

CHERI often delivers the greatest value when:

- Existing C or C++ software is expensive to replace
- Products are widely deployed or difficult to update
- Systems are expected to operate for many years
- Software handles sensitive data or critical functions
- Security incidents have significant operational or financial consequences

The case may be weaker where software is already memory-safe, strong isolation mechanisms already exist, or the protected code has limited access to valuable assets.

## A Long-Term Investment in Resilience
{: id="a-long-term-investment-in-resilience" }

CHERI is not a replacement for good development processes, testing, updates, monitoring, or other cybersecurity controls. Its value comes from addressing one of the most persistent sources of software vulnerability while preserving existing software investments.

For organisations building products that must remain secure, reliable, and supportable for years to come, CHERI can create long-term value by reducing risk, lowering operational burden, strengthening assurance, and extending the life of critical software assets.

data.title: The Strategic Case for CHERI
data.summary: CHERI helps reduce risk, protect software investments, build trust and create competitive advantage.

pages.body:
CHERI helps prevent many memory-safety vulnerabilities by design, creating the foundations for more secure and resilient systems.

Organisations face growing pressure to improve cybersecurity, strengthen resilience, and demonstrate secure-by-design practices. Yet many critical systems still depend on large bodies of existing software that cannot simply be replaced.

CHERI offers a practical approach. By adding hardware-enforced memory protection and compartmentalisation, it helps reduce the impact of memory-safety vulnerabilities while preserving the value of existing software investments.

## Reduce Risk
{: id="reduce-risk" }

CHERI can help reduce cyber risk by addressing one of the most persistent classes of software vulnerabilities at the hardware level. It supports secure-by-design objectives, strengthens critical systems, and helps create a more resilient digital ecosystem.

Cyberattacks impose enormous costs on organisations worldwide, disrupting services, delaying operations, damaging trust, and creating financial losses. Most importantly, they have reached a scale where national security can be impacted.

Investing in stronger security is a way to reduce that risk, at any level:

- Less operational risk for technology users
- Less risk of disrupting development or sales for product developers
- Reduced national cyber risk for governments

Reducing risk is not only about preventing incidents. It is also about reducing uncertainty and improving confidence in the systems your organisation depends on.

## Preserve Investment
{: id="preserve-investment" }

Many organisations and products rely on software that has been developed, tested, and maintained over many years. Replacing this software is often expensive, disruptive, or impractical.

CHERI is designed to **strengthen existing software** rather than require a complete rewrite. Rather than replacing proven software, organisations can often strengthen and modernise it incrementally, allowing them to improve security while continuing to benefit from established processes and accumulated expertise.

CHERI can help organisations:

- Extend the life of existing software assets
- Protect previous engineering investments
- Make new products and platforms more durable

Rather than choosing between accepting risk and rewriting everything, CHERI provides a third option: strengthen what already exists.

## Build Trust
{: id="build-trust" }

Customers, regulators, governments, and insurers increasingly expect products and services to be secure by design. Organisations must not only improve security, but also demonstrate that appropriate protections are in place.

CHERI provides security mechanisms that are enforced by hardware, making protection stronger, measurable, and easier to demonstrate. This can support assurance activities, strengthen security claims, and increase confidence among stakeholders.

The result can be:

- Greater customer confidence
- Stronger security assurance
- Support for regulatory and procurement expectations
- Improved product and brand reputation
- A clearer demonstration of secure-by-design principles

Trust is difficult to build and easy to lose. Stronger foundations can help organisations protect both their systems and their reputation.

## Create Competitive Advantage
{: id="create-competitive-advantage" }

Security is increasingly influencing purchasing decisions, procurement requirements, and regulatory expectations. Organisations that **invest early** in stronger security foundations can be better positioned to meet future customer expectations and secure-by-design requirements.

Depending on their role, organisations or their customers may benefit from:

- Lower ownership and maintenance costs
- Reduced disruption from security incidents
- Stronger product differentiation
- Increased customer confidence
- Better alignment with emerging security regulations
- Access to new markets and opportunities

As security expectations continue to rise, investing in resilient technologies today can help organisations prepare for tomorrow’s requirements.

## A Strategic Investment in Resilience
{: id="a-strategic-investment-in-resilience" }

CHERI is more than a security technology. It helps organisations reduce risk, protect software investments, build trust, and prepare for future security expectations. For organisations seeking stronger security without discarding decades of software development, CHERI offers a practical path towards more resilient products and services.

data.summary: CHERI can support infrastructure resilience by preventing or limiting attacks.

pages.body:
Critical infrastructure depends on services that society cannot easily function without. Disruption to energy, water, transport, healthcare, communications, or industrial systems can have consequences far beyond a single organisation.

CHERI cannot provide service resilience by itself, but it can strengthen the technical foundations underneath it.

Cybersecurity frameworks such as European Union’s [NIS2 directive](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/nis2-directive) increasingly emphasise resilience, risk management, and the protection of essential services. These goals align closely with reducing the impact of software vulnerabilities and limiting the consequences of compromise.

The growing importance of memory safety is also reflected in **ETSI TS 104 198 Memory Safety** standard, which defines multiple levels of memory-safety assurance and recognises CHERI as one of the strongest approaches.

## Memory Safety and resilience
{: id="memory-safety-and-resilience" }

Essential systems often contain native code, specialist devices, supplier components, and long replacement cycles. Some software remains in operation for decades. A recurring memory vulnerability can therefore affect systems that are difficult to patch, replace, or take offline.

Conventional mitigations reduce the likelihood of successful exploitation, but they may still allow the invalid access to occur, with potentially damaging and irreversible consequences. CHERI changes that boundary by allowing the processor to enforce what software can access and what it is allowed to do.

This can lead to:

- **Reducing the likelihood** of compromise
- **Limiting the impact** of compromise

The distinction is important in infrastructure. Preventing every attack is unrealistic, while preventing one compromised component from reaching an essential function can still preserve part of the service.

## Where CHERI can fit infrastructure policy
{: id="where-cheri-can-fit-infrastructure-policy" }

CHERI can be relevant to industrial gateways, control systems, communications equipment, remote-management platforms, monitoring infrastructure, update services, and safety-related embedded devices. These components often process untrusted data while holding access to more sensitive systems.

It is also relevant to constrained controllers where conventional process isolation is unavailable, and to consolidated systems where software of different trust levels shares one processor.

Because CHERI can protect existing C and C++ software, it offers a route that aligns with **gradual infrastructure renewal**. Capability-aware components can appear in new equipment while older protocols and neighbouring systems remain in service.

## Resilience beyond containment
{: id="resilience-beyond-containment" }

A capability fault prevents an unauthorised memory operation, but it may stop the affected component. Availability then depends on the wider design: redundancy, restart, failover, safe degradation, logging, and recovery.

Network segmentation, identity, secure configuration, monitoring, backups, incident response, supply-chain assurance, physical protection, and manual alternatives also remain necessary. CHERI adds an internal boundary; it does not replace the layers around it.

## More meaningful security claims
{: id="more-meaningful-security-claims" }

Policy and assurance benefit when a technology claim describes an outcome. “The protocol parser cannot access control state” identifies a boundary that can be represented and tested. “The device uses CHERI” does not reveal how much software is protected or what remains reachable.

As governments and operators place greater emphasis on resilience, the ability to contain failures becomes increasingly important, especially for critical infrastructure. CHERI helps reduce the impact of memory vulnerabilities and strengthens separation between critical functions, supporting more resilient digital infrastructure without requiring complete replacement of existing software.

data.summary: Regulators increasingly expect security-by-design, resilience and effective risk management – CHERI can support those.

pages.body:
As cybersecurity regulation shifts from reactive security measures toward **secure-by-design** products, technologies that reduce vulnerability exposure become increasingly valuable.

CHERI can be relevant because memory safety and containment affect those outcomes. It can reduce exposure to a recurring vulnerability class and provide technical evidence that a component’s access is restricted. It does not, by itself, establish compliance.

The growing focus on memory safety is also reflected in standards activity. **ETSI TS 104 198 Memory Safety** defines multiple levels of memory-safety assurance and highlights CHERI as one of the technologies that can contribute to achieving the highest levels of memory-safety protection.

## European Union Cyber Resilience Act
{: id="european-union-cyber-resilience-act" }

The [Cyber Resilience Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act) covers products with digital elements placed on the European Union market. It introduces cybersecurity requirements across planning, design, development, maintenance, vulnerability handling, and information supplied with products.

The Act entered into force on 10 December 2024. Its reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026, and its main obligations apply from 11 December 2027.

CHERI may contribute to reducing product risk by preventing many invalid memory accesses and containing selected components. The Act also covers activities that CHERI does not provide, including cybersecurity risk assessment, vulnerability handling, support periods, documentation, reporting, and conformity assessment.

## United Kingdom consumer connectable products
{: id="united-kingdom-consumer-connectable-products" }

The UK’s [Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure product-security regime](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-uk-product-security-and-telecommunications-infrastructure-product-security-regime) has applied since 29 April 2024. It places duties on manufacturers, importers, and distributors of relevant consumer connectable products and sets baseline requirements concerning passwords, vulnerability reporting, and information about security-update periods.

CHERI is not a requirement of that regime. Its relevance is indirect but practical: connected products often contain memory-unsafe firmware and exposed protocol code, and capability protection can reduce the risk that one malformed input leads to wider access inside the device.

## NIS2 and Essential Services
{: id="nis2-and-essential-services" }

The European Union’s [NIS2 framework](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/nis2-directive) addresses cybersecurity risk management and incident reporting for covered sectors and entities. National implementation determines the exact obligations.

For essential and important services, CHERI can contribute to prevention and containment inside devices, gateways, infrastructure software, and operational systems. Availability, recovery, supply-chain security, monitoring, and incident management remain broader service properties.

## How CHERI can support compliance evidence
{: id="how-cheri-can-support-compliance-evidence" }

A CHERI implementation can provide evidence at several levels:

- Demonstrating stronger memory protection
- Demonstrating restricted component authority
- Demonstrating compartment boundaries
- Demonstrating blocked invalid accesses
- Documenting assumptions and limitations

That evidence can support a wider account of secure design and risk reduction. It does not replace legal interpretation or establish that every requirement has been met.

## Important Limitations
{: id="important-limitations" }

CHERI contributes to memory safety and compartmentalisation, but products must still meet broader requirements covering updates, vulnerability management, incident reporting, support, documentation, governance, and regulatory obligations.

## Supporting regulatory objectives
{: id="supporting-regulatory-objectives" }

Cybersecurity regulation increasingly encourages organisations to reduce risk and build security into products from the outset. While CHERI is not a compliance mechanism, it can support regulatory objectives by reducing exposure to memory vulnerabilities, strengthening isolation between components, and helping organisations demonstrate secure-by-design engineering practices.

data.summary: Policy makers, regulators, and cybersecurity agencies are pushing for safer software foundations.

pages.body:
**Memory vulnerabilities** remain a major source of software security risk, prompting governments to encourage safer software and stronger resilience.

This policy direction creates a clear place for CHERI. Memory-safe languages can prevent broad classes of errors in new code. CHERI can bring hardware-enforced memory protection to existing software and support **secure-by-design** and **resilience** objectives.

## The direction of public guidance
{: id="the-direction-of-public-guidance" }

[CISA’s Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/case-memory-safe-roadmaps) presents memory safety as a strategic responsibility for software manufacturers. It focuses on measurable plans for reducing reliance on memory-unsafe languages and making progress visible to customers.

[CISA’s work on critical open-source projects](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2024/06/26/cisa-and-partners-release-guidance-exploring-memory-safety-critical-open-source-projects) also recognises that widely used dependencies form part of the exposure. This is important because a product may contain native code that its own development team did not write.

The UK National Cyber Security Centre describes memory-safe languages and hardware approaches as parts of a wider secure-by-design landscape. Its discussion of [raising software resilience at scale](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/raising-cyber-resilience-software-at-scale) identifies CHERI as one of the technology approaches that can contribute to a more resilient ecosystem.

The UK’s [Digital Security by Design programme](https://www.ukri.org/what-we-do/browse-our-areas-of-investment-and-support/digital-security-by-design/) provided a major public investment in CHERI research, the Morello platform, software, and industrial evaluation.

## Where CHERI adds to the policy picture
{: id="where-cheri-adds-to-the-policy-picture" }

Much public guidance focuses on increasing the use of memory-safe languages. CHERI addresses a complementary challenge: improving the security of existing software, operating systems, firmware, and infrastructure that will continue to rely on C and C++ for years to come.

CHERI can contribute in two ways:

- **Reducing the impact** of memory vulnerabilities through processor-enforced memory protection.
- **Limiting the consequences** of compromise through stronger compartmentalisation between components.

These properties support policy goals around secure-by-design products, vulnerability reduction, resilience, and the protection of legacy investment. They also make CHERI complementary to language migration rather than a competing universal answer, as explained in [CHERI and Rust](/discover/why-cheri/cheri-and-rust/).

## CHERI’s role in memory safety
{: id="cheris-role-in-memory-safety" }

**ETSI TS 104 198 Memory Safety** standard defines several levels of memory safety, recognising that different systems may require different protections. The **highest level**, and CHERI, may be particularly relevant for systems requiring the strongest memory-safety assurance, including critical infrastructure, safety-critical environments, and systems handling sensitive data.

The world’s software infrastructure contains vast amounts of existing C and C++ code that cannot realistically and economically be replaced overnight.

CHERI’s policy relevance lies in providing a much stronger solution to memory safety. It offers a way to cover software that might otherwise remain dependent on exploit mitigations alone, and it adds containment when preventing every defect is unrealistic.

## Guidance, standards, and law
{: id="guidance-standards-and-law" }

As governments and cybersecurity authorities place increasing emphasis on memory safety, CHERI provides a practical way to strengthen existing software while supporting secure-by-design and resilience goals. It complements memory-safe languages, helps protect software investments, and expands the range of options available to product developers.

pages.body:
The CHERI ecosystem includes several organisations with complementary missions. The CHERI Research Centre, The Capable Hub, and the CHERI Alliance each play different roles, but work closely together to help turn CHERI research into practical products, open-source software, standards, and real-world deployment.

![CHERI Alliance, CHERI Research Centre and The Capable Hub working together](/assets/shared/source-assets/9540283f8f64-ca-crc-tch.png){: .image-full }

## Strengthening the CHERI Ecosystem Together
{: id="strengthening-the-cheri-ecosystem-together" }

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ![CHERI Logo](/assets/shared/branding/9899bc30b0-logo-blue.webp){: .image-full } | **The CHERI Alliance**  Coordinating the global CHERI ecosystem |

The CHERI Alliance helps coordinate the global CHERI ecosystem by bringing together industry, academia, government, and open-source communities.

Our role includes:

- Organising collaboration through working groups, community events, and conferences such as CHERI Blossoms and CHERITech.
- Supporting ecosystem alignment through standards activities, certification, and technical guidance.
- Promoting CHERI adoption through education, outreach, and community engagement.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ![The Capable Hub logo](/assets/shared/source-assets/70ab53193721-the-capable-hub.png){: .image-full } | **The Capable Hub** Engineering open-source CHERI software |

[The Capable Hub](/organisations/the-capable-hub/) provides engineering expertise, infrastructure, and open-source software that help organisations build and deploy CHERI-enabled products.

Key contributions include:

- Developing and maintaining CHERI-enabled open-source software and supporting upstream adoption.
- Providing shared engineering infrastructure, including CI systems and hardware-in-the-loop testing.
- Helping mature research software and prototypes into reusable components for real-world deployment.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ![CHERI Research Centre logo](/assets/shared/source-assets/171acadadd69-cheri-research-centre.png){: .image-full } | **The CHERI Research Centre** Advancing CHERI through world leading research |

The [CHERI Research Centre](https://cheri.cst.cam.ac.uk) at the [University of Cambridge](/organisations/university-of-cambridge/) has led CHERI research for more than fifteen years.

Its contributions include:

- Advancing CHERI architecture, software, prototyping, and standards development.
- Collaborating with industry to ensure research reflects real-world needs.
- Exploring new directions for CHERI technology and memory-safe computing.

## From research to adoption
{: id="from-research-to-adoption" }

- The CHERI Research Centre develops new concepts, architectures, and technologies.
- The Capable Hub helps turn research into robust software, tooling, infrastructure, and reusable components.
- The CHERI Alliance connects those technologies with adopters, standards activities, certification, education, and the wider ecosystem.

### Shared goals
{: id="shared-goals" }

Together, the three organisations:

- Accelerate CHERI adoption across industry, academia, and open source.
- Support the development of reliable CHERI-enabled software, platforms, and products.
- Help move secure computing technologies from research into real-world deployment.

Interested in helping shape the future of memory-safe computing? [Join the CHERI Alliance](/alliance/membership/contact/)!

data.summary: Collaboration, openness, and shared effort are at the heart of CHERI adoption.

pages.body:
The CHERI Alliance exists because no single organisation can build a secure computing ecosystem alone. Hardware vendors, software developers, researchers, standards bodies, governments, educators, integrators, and users all have an important role to play.

**Collaboration** is therefore one of the Alliance’s core principles. Wherever practical, we aim to help organisations work together on shared challenges while allowing each participant to maintain ownership of its own products, projects, and priorities.

## Open by default
{: id="open-by-default" }

The Alliance believes that accelerating CHERI adoption requires a strong foundation of shared knowledge, open resources, and collaborative development.

Whenever practical, Alliance outputs are developed openly and made publicly available so the wider ecosystem can benefit. This helps avoid duplicated effort, encourages participation, and allows organisations to focus their resources on the areas that differentiate their products and services.

Examples include:

- educational material and tutorials
- technical guidance, recommendations and standards-related material
- software demonstrations and examples
- community resources and outreach material
- shared compliance and test assets
- contributions to open-source projects

The Alliance aims to make outputs open whenever practical, but some discussions, planning activities, and collaborative work may take place within member-only groups before being released publicly, or even stay internal. This balance allows organisations to collaborate effectively while ensuring that the wider ecosystem benefits from the results.

## Choosing the right licence
{: id="choosing-the-right-licence" }

Different types of collaboration have different requirements. The Alliance therefore applies licences that best support the intended use of each resource.

In general:

- Educational material, tutorials, outreach content, and technical recommendations are normally released under an open Creative Commons licence - preferably [CC-BY-SA](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) ![CC-BY-SA](/assets/shared/source-assets/bacc656ec8f4-cc-by-sa.webp){: .image-left .image-inline }
- Software examples, compliance assets, and technical contributions are normally released under permissive open-source licences to encourage adoption and contribution
- Contributions made to existing external projects generally retain the licence of that project
- Internal member discussions and confidential information remain protected where required
- The CHERI® trademark remains protected and subject to the [Trademark Policy](/policies/trademark-policy/)

The goal is simple: maximise reuse and collaboration while respecting legitimate confidentiality, ownership, and operational requirements.

## Collaboration without losing ownership
{: id="collaboration-without-losing-ownership" }

Participation in the Alliance does not require organisations to give up ownership of their products, research, or intellectual property. Our [IP Policy](/policies/intellectual-property-policy/) has been designed to recognise each member’s IP and support collaboration while helping ensure that CHERI Alliance standards can be implemented without unreasonable licensing barriers.

Where collaboration creates shared resources, the preferred approach is to make those outputs openly available whenever practical.

This allows organisations to **collaborate on common challenges** without losing control of the technologies that differentiate their own products and services.

## Sharing benefits everyone
{: id="sharing-benefits-everyone" }

Collaborative development creates benefits across the ecosystem:

- Reduced duplication of effort
- Faster adoption of CHERI technology
- Better interoperability across platforms
- Stronger educational resources
- Shared solutions to common problems
- Increased visibility for participating organisations

By working together on shared foundations, Alliance members can spend more time innovating and less time solving the same problems independently. This alignment work also creates opportunities for vendors to create solutions that would be compatible with multiple vendors, hence enabling profitable markets that ultimately benefit CHERI adoption.

## Collaborating beyond membership
{: id="collaborating-beyond-membership" }

On some projects, in particular for open-source software, the CHERI Alliance working groups also collaborate more widely with open-source communities. This pragmatic approach helps ensure that projects progress as fast as possible, without waiting for all participants to become members.

The goal is to accelerate progress across the ecosystem, not to create barriers to participation.

pages.body:
CHERI adoption grows when trusted community members can explain the technology in ways that resonate with developers, researchers, industry professionals, educators, and policymakers. The Ambassador Programme supports people who want to help make those connections.

## What ambassadors do
{: id="what-ambassadors-do" }

Ambassadors choose activities that match their interests, skills, and availability. These may include:

- writing tutorials, articles, demonstrations, or technical papers
- giving talks and creating video or presentation material
- sharing accurate news and practical experience
- helping with conferences, workshops, and online events
- introducing organisations and communities to the Alliance
- Mentoring newcomers and supporting community projects
- Providing feedback on educational materials and outreach activities

Ambassadors act in accordance with Alliance policies and programme guidance. The role does not make an ambassador a governing-board member, product certifier, or official spokesperson for the entire Alliance.

## What the programme offers
{: id="what-the-programme-offers" }

The programme provides opportunities to:

- Connect with the global CHERI community
- Participate in working groups and technical discussions
- Access community resources, events, and briefings
- Contribute to projects and outreach activities
- Gain recognition for community contributions
- Help shape the future of the CHERI ecosystem

Specific benefits and participation requirements may evolve as the programme develops.

## Joining the programme
{: id="joining-the-programme" }

The programme is open to people with a genuine interest in CHERI, cybersecurity, and community engagement. Applicants should be active within a relevant technical, research, industry, education, or regional community and interested in helping others learn about CHERI.

Participation begins with an application and review process, followed by onboarding for successful applicants.

Apply or request more information through the [Alliance contact page](/alliance/membership/contact/).

pages.body:
## Contact form
{: id="contact-webform-title" }

Use the enquiry form below to explore the contact options. This preview does not send messages.

[Open the published Alliance contact form](https://cheri-alliance.org/contact/#contact_form).

## Help us route your message
{: id="help-us-route-your-message" }

Use a clear subject and include the relevant detail:

- **Membership:** include the organisation, location, interest in CHERI, and intended participation.
- **Working group:** include the topic, relevant experience, and the contribution or question.
- **CHERI Enabled:** include the product name, version, organisation, and intended application timing.
- **Events or speakers:** include the audience, format, date, location, topic, and expected attendance.
- **Media:** include the publication, deadline, question, and requested spokesperson or area of expertise.
- **Trademark or brand:** include the mark, material, territory, intended use, and publication date.
- **Technical resource:** include the platform, software version, goal, and resources already consulted.

Do not send passwords, private keys, export-controlled material, vulnerability details, or other sensitive information in an initial general enquiry. Ask for an appropriate handling route first.

For a potential security vulnerability in a particular product or project, follow that vendor’s or project’s published security-reporting process. The Alliance does not maintain every CHERI implementation.

Policy documents and programme pages may already answer formal questions. Linking the page you consulted will help the team identify whether clarification or an update is needed.

pages.body:
![CHERI Alliance member logo](/assets/shared/source-assets/edeb264ff3b7-cheri-member.webp){: .image-left }

CHERI Alliance membership connects you with companies, researchers and practitioners working across the CHERI ecosystem. Whether you want to influence its direction, learn from experts, increase your visibility or simply demonstrate your support for CHERI, there is a way to get involved.

Organisations can join as Full Members or eligible Community Members, while individuals can participate as Community Members or Ambassadors.

## Benefits of membership
{: id="benefits-of-membership" }

CHERI Alliance members can:

- **Connect** with companies, researchers and practitioners across the CHERI ecosystem
- **Collaborate** through [working groups](/alliance/leadership/working-groups/), [events](/news-and-events/events-and-archive/upcoming-events/) and shared activities
- **Learn** from CHERI experts and real-world implementation experience
- **Influence** technical priorities, standards and activities that accelerate adoption
- **Gain visibility** through member profiles, events, publications, product listings and Alliance communications
- **Contribute** to software, guidance, education and outreach
- **Demonstrate support** for CHERI and help build industry confidence and demand
- **Participate in governance**, including [Governing Board](/alliance/leadership/governing-board/) elections

See [Why Join?](/alliance/membership/why-join/) for more about the value of becoming a CHERI Alliance member.

## Participate at your own pace
{: id="participate-at-your-own-pace" }

Membership does not require a minimum level of participation, except for Ambassadors, who commit to supporting Alliance activities.

How much you participate is **entirely up to you**. Join the working groups, events and activities that match your interests and priorities. If enough members want to collaborate on a new topic, the Alliance usually create new working groups or activities around it.

Even simply becoming a member matters. A growing membership demonstrates demand for CHERI and encourages suppliers, developers and adopters to invest in the technology.

## Membership for organisations
{: id="membership-for-organisations" }

There are two organisational membership options.

**Full Membership** is for **commercial** organisations and others seeking the highest level of visibility, influence and membership benefits.

**Community Membership** is a free option for eligible research organisations, public bodies, non-profits and open-source organisations.

### Full membership
{: id="full-membership" }

Full Membership is designed for organisations that want the highest level of participation, visibility and influence within the CHERI ecosystem.

Commercial organisations join as Full Members. Research organisations, public bodies, non-profits and open-source organisations can also choose Full Membership for its additional benefits.

Full Members receive:

- Greater **visibility** through a dedicated member page, Alliance communications, conferences, publications, speaking opportunities and promotional activities
- Greater **influence** in Alliance governance, including nominating candidates and electing the majority of [Governing Board](/alliance/leadership/governing-board/) representatives
- Reduced certification fees for CHERI [product certification](/adopt/assurance-and-adoption/certification/)
- Access to all working groups, with no mandatory level of participation
- Use of the applicable CHERI Alliance membership mark

### Community membership
{: id="community-membership" }

Community Membership is available **free of charge** to eligible research organisations, public bodies, non-profits and open-source organisations that want to participate in and contribute to the CHERI ecosystem.

Community Members can:

- participate in working groups, events and Alliance activities
- connect and collaborate across the CHERI ecosystem
- receive a dedicated member page
- contribute to research, open source, education, public policy and adoption
- vote for Community representatives on the Governing Board
- stand for available Community seats

Community Members are an important part of the Alliance, bringing together organisations whose work helps broaden and strengthen the CHERI ecosystem.

## Membership for individuals
{: id="membership-for-individuals" }

### Individual Community Members
{: id="individual-community-members" }

Individuals can join as Community Members to contribute expertise, participate in the community and engage with Alliance activities.

### Ambassadors
{: id="ambassadors" }

Ambassadors are Community Members who make an additional commitment to support the Alliance through education, outreach, events, content creation and community building.

## Membership fees
{: id="membership-fees" }

![DCMS Logo](/assets/shared/source-assets/62e58da9da64-dcms-s.webp){: .image-left }

The CHERI Alliance is a lean, **non-profit** organisation. Membership fees support its collaboration infrastructure, communications, events and other activities that help accelerate CHERI adoption.

We deliberately keep fees accessible because a broad and diverse membership strengthens the CHERI ecosystem. This is possible thanks to the support from the [UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS)](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-for-digital-culture-media-and-sport).

**Community Membership is free** for eligible organisations and individuals.

### Full Membership

| Company size (nb employees) | Annual membership fee (see below for discounts) |
| --- | ---: |
| 0 – 5 | £ 800 |
| 5 – 25 | £ 2,500 |
| 25 – 50 | £ 4,000 |
| 50 –250 | £ 8,000 |
| 250 + | £ 16,000 |

**Additional discounts** are available for **multi-year** memberships and successful member **referrals**, and discounts can be combined.

[Contact us](/alliance/membership/contact/) for details.

## Ready to get involved?
{: id="ready-to-get-involved" }

Join the organisations, researchers and individuals building the CHERI ecosystem and helping move CHERI towards widespread adoption.

Whether you want to participate actively, increase your organisation's visibility or simply demonstrate your support for CHERI, there is a membership option for you.

[Contact us](/alliance/membership/contact/) to discuss the best way to get involved.
